utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce to help cover disposal costs.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for imposing it?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A second reason is that a levy would encourage retailers to reduce unnecessary plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Some retailers say the levy would punish businesses that already operate on narrow profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But that concern targets the wrong policy: the levy would target avoidable packaging rather than every package used by retailers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the levy cover protective wrapping as well as decorative wrapping?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: It should apply only to plastic packaging that is unnecessary for protecting or transporting fresh produce.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you mean that the levy would not apply to every piece of plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers could avoid the levy by switching to reusable crates and lighter packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, retailers could escape the levy by using reusable crates and less packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Consumers should not bear the cost of unnecessary packaging through higher produce prices.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Elif is saying that shoppers should not pay for plastic packaging that retailers could avoid.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A levy based on packaging weight would be the simplest system to administer, because retailers can record packaging weight more easily than they can classify every design feature.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I buy fresh berries from a local shop every week. Retailers already record packaging weight for some supplier audits.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy can be collected through existing packaging-data reports, because most large retailers already submit those reports to regulators.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, existing packaging-data reports can be used to collect the levy, which is why retailers should pay it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you support the proposal if the levy excluded genuinely necessary packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I prefer buying loose apples when the shop has them.

utterances.text: Plenty of people keep old phones in drawers for a decade or more.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: That matters, because the deposit only works if people actually return devices instead of hoarding them.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: They would return them, since the money would be sitting there waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: I bought my own laptop back in 2019, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: Many countries now publish yearly statistics on electronic waste.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Should people be expected to return online purchases to physical shops?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes, people should be expected to return online purchases to physical shops. I worked in a retail shop during university.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: But that expectation is unfair, because many physical shops lack the space and staff to handle online returns.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Because people should be expected to return online purchases to physical shops, a shared shop-based return system would reduce packaging and delivery journeys.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Online returns often require customers to print labels and arrange collection. Local shops would give customers a nearby place to return online purchases, and that is why the expectation is reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is to use local shops as nearby return points for online purchases?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Exactly. Because online returns often require customers to print labels and arrange collection, online returns are cumbersome for many customers. That is why people should be expected to use physical shops.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Most physical shops already have staffed customer-service counters, because those customer-service counters could handle modest return volumes.

utterances.text: The arrangement remains workable because a staggered schedule could give teachers predictable groups of students. That works because predictable student groups would let teachers plan lessons more effectively.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: A shared attendance app could assign students to start-time groups automatically; because of that, teachers could plan around those groups, which is why schools can offer the choice. I have two younger siblings who attend primary school.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Item four: satellite internet subsidies. Chloe, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think governments should not subsidise satellite internet for households without reliable broadband. Many rural households simply will not get any fixed-line connection in the next five years.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: But it would be wasted money, since fibre will reach most of those homes eventually.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: So you are saying, Josefa, that a satellite subsidy is short-term spending that fibre will make obsolete?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Still, I accept that the rollout in remote areas has slipped by years more than once.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: My cousin runs a clinic that lost patient records during a storm last summer.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Fine, then satellite could be a bridge for households until fibre arrives, because satellite subsidies would be wasted money, since fibre will reach most of those homes eventually.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Put another way, it is a temporary measure that ends when fibre arrives.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: We could limit it to the dish and installation, since a one-off equipment subsidy would cost far less than paying monthly subscriptions.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Another reason against subsidising satellite internet for those households, I should add, is that children in homes without broadband fall behind in schoolwork.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Noted. Separately, the council should hold the next meeting in the town hall.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Satellite dishes need a clear view of the sky to work.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes. Aiko, you first.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: They should not ban it, because trial releases have cut local dengue-carrying mosquito populations by over ninety percent. That result is hard to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Dalia, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: I do, and the reason is simple: a release cannot be recalled once the mosquitoes have spread into the wild. So governments should ban it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Aiko, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: But the modified mosquitoes die out after a few generations, so the change does not persist.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Aiko, you are saying the modified mosquitoes do not persist in the wild.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: I should say I work for a public health agency.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Helga, go on.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Bed nets and spraying have failed to stop dengue in many cities, which shows other methods are not enough on their own.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Other mosquito species could fill the empty niche.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: In other words, removing one mosquito species could have knock-on effects on the ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Those effects are unproven and speculative, since the concerns are theoretical rather than demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: My own village had a dengue outbreak last year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo, any last point?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Communities near release sites should vote on trials, since local consent is needed before any release.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Dengue is most common in tropical and subtropical regions.

props.text: Governments should not ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes.

A release cannot be recalled once the modified mosquitoes have spread into the wild.
Governments should ban the release of modified mosquitoes.
The modified mosquitoes die out after a few generations, so the change does not persist.
Dalia says the modified mosquitoes do not persist in the wild.
Helga does not work for a public health agency.
Bed nets and spraying have failed to stop dengue in many cities.
Other methods of disease control are not enough on their own.
Other mosquito species could fill the empty ecological niche.
Removing one mosquito species could have knock-on effects on the ecosystem.
The ecosystem effects of removing a mosquito species are unproven and speculative.
Pablo's own village had a dengue outbreak last year.
Communities near release sites should be allowed to vote on the trials.
The debate has run well over its scheduled time.
Concerns about ecosystem effects are theoretical rather than demonstrated.
Local consent is needed before any release.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes. Aiko, you first.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: They should not ban it, because trial releases have cut local dengue-carrying mosquito populations by over ninety percent. That result is hard to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Dalia, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: I do, and the reason is simple: a release cannot be recalled once the mosquitoes have spread into the wild. So governments should ban it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Aiko, a reply?

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: But the modified mosquitoes die out within a few generations, so the change does not last.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Aiko, you are saying the modified mosquitoes do not persist in the wild.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: I should say I work for a public health agency.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Helga, go on.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Bed nets and spraying have failed to stop dengue in many cities, which shows other methods are not enough on their own.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Other mosquito species could fill the empty niche.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: In other words, removing one mosquito species could have knock-on effects on the ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Those effects are unproven and speculative, since the concerns are theoretical rather than demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: My own village had a dengue outbreak last year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pablo, any last point?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Communities near release sites should vote on trials, since local consent is needed before any release.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, I believe terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because competent adults have authority over their own bodies and the manner of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some patients have pain that palliative care simply cannot relieve, and that is why I say forcing them to endure it is cruel. Which is another reason the law should allow them to request help.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Safeguards such as requiring two independent doctors make coercion much easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has operated with such safeguards since 1997, which shows they work. Put another way, coercion is far easier to spot when two independent doctors must agree on a request.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some people say good palliative care makes assisted dying unnecessary. But even the best hospices cannot relieve every patient's suffering, that is to say, medicine has limits.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I volunteered at a hospice for six years. The patients I met mostly wanted control over how their last days went, which shows how much people value authority over their own dying.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Legalising it would not oblige anyone to use it, since the right is only a right to request. In other words, nobody would be forced to take it up.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The bill debated last year ran to eleven pages, for what it is worth. Opponents say elderly and vulnerable people could feel pressured into choosing death.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Public opinion supports it too, because recent polls show a large majority of British adults in favour. The reason for that is that legalising it would not oblige anyone to use it, since the right is only a right to request.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: To sum up, patients deserve a lawful choice at the end of life.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, I believe terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because competent adults have authority over their own bodies and the manner of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some patients have pain that palliative care simply cannot relieve, and that is why I say forcing them to endure it is cruel. Which is another reason the law should allow them to request help.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Opponents say elderly and vulnerable people could feel pressured into choosing death. But safeguards such as requiring two independent doctors make coercion much easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has operated with such safeguards since 1997, which shows they work. Put another way, coercion is far easier to spot when two independent doctors must agree on a request.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some people say good palliative care makes assisted dying unnecessary. But even the best hospices cannot relieve every patient's suffering, that is to say, medicine has limits.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Most of the hospice patients I met wanted control over how their last days went, which shows how much people value authority over their own dying.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Legalising it would not oblige anyone to use it, since the right is only a right to request. In other words, nobody would be forced to take it up.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The bill debated last year ran to eleven pages, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Public opinion supports it too, because recent polls show a large majority of British adults in favour.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Patients deserve a lawful choice at the end of life, and that is why terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Item two is mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences. Emeka, will you open?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: I think we should abolish them, and the reason is that they remove judges' discretion to consider the circumstances of each offender.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: That discretion matters because low-level couriers often get the same sentence as the organisers of drug rings. Which is why I call minimums unfair to people who played only a minor role.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Can anyone give figures on prison capacity?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Prisons in the region are at 130 percent of capacity.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Long mandatory sentences for drug offences keep prison populations high, so abolishing minimums would reduce overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: But abolishing them would make sentences for serious traffickers too lenient.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Sorry, we are running behind schedule, I think. Still, judges can already hand down heavy sentences on traffickers without a minimum, so they can be trusted to be severe.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Fixed minimums do deter people from joining supply networks.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Studies find no clear deterrent effect from longer fixed minimums, which shows deterrence is a weak ground.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: So, to answer you, Zainab: removing minimums would not make serious traffickers' sentences too lenient.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying that judges should be free to weigh each offender's circumstances, and that minimums treat couriers and ringleaders alike.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Noted. The Home Office report on sentencing is due in March.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Then, in other words, the committee should recommend abolishing mandatory minimums for drug offences.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Item two is mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences. Emeka, will you open?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: I think we should abolish them, and the reason is that they remove judges' discretion to consider the circumstances of each offender.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: That discretion matters because low-level couriers often get the same sentence as the organisers of drug rings. Which is why I call minimums unfair to people who played only a minor role.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Can anyone give figures on prison capacity?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Prisons in the region are at 130 percent of capacity.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Long mandatory sentences for drug offences keep prison populations high, so abolishing minimums would reduce overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: But abolishing them would make sentences for serious traffickers too lenient.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Sorry, we are running late, I think. Still, judges can already impose heavy sentences on traffickers without a minimum, so they can be trusted to be severe.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Fixed minimums do deter people from joining supply networks.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Research on drug sentencing has not found a clear deterrent effect from longer fixed minimums, which shows deterrence is a weak ground.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: So, to answer you, Zainab: removing minimums would not make serious traffickers' sentences too lenient.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying that judges should be free to weigh each offender's circumstances, and that minimums treat couriers and ringleaders alike.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Noted. The Home Office report on sentencing is due in March.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Then, in other words, the committee should recommend abolishing mandatory minimums for drug offences.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Our question is whether employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement. Yusuf, make the case for it.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Many employers currently omit salary ranges from job advertisements. Publishing salary ranges would let applicants compare opportunities before applying.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Arjun, what is the strongest objection?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Arjun has worked in recruitment for eight years. I worry that a badly designed rule could create false confidence.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Publishing salary ranges would reduce applications from people who cannot accept the available pay, and it would make unjustified pay differences within a company easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Arjun, does a range solve the problem if the range is broad?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Employers can use very wide salary ranges to conceal the pay they actually intend to offer, so very wide salary ranges can mislead applicants instead of helping them compare jobs.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: So you are saying that wide salary ranges can make advertised pay information misleading.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A legal minimum width for salary ranges is workable, and that requirement would make published salary ranges more consistent across employers.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: So you are proposing a rule that requires salary ranges to be wide enough to support meaningful comparison.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, and publishing salary ranges would make unjustified differences in employees' pay more visible.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Private salary negotiations can protect applicants who have unusual skills or circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: In other words, your concern is that private negotiation can protect applicants with unusual skills or circumstances.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: My conclusion is that employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement, because ranges let applicants compare opportunities, reduce unsuitable applications, expose unjustified pay differences, and become genuinely comparable when a minimum-width rule applies.

utterances.text: Producers should not pay a methane tax based on herd emissions, since cattle and sheep are a leading source of human-caused methane and right now producers face no charge for it.

utterances.text: But a methane tax would push up meat prices for ordinary households.

utterances.text: I grew up on a dairy farm, so I know how thin the margins are. Still, the revenue could be handed back to households as a rebate, which answers the price worry.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: A rebate, hmm. How would that be paid out?

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Put another way, households would be compensated for the higher meat prices.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Maybe, but there is a bigger problem: measuring emissions herd by herd is too costly for small farms.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: I haven't read the latest government report on methane monitoring, so I can't say how costly it is. What do you propose instead?

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: I'd say the tax would be unfair to small farms, because the measuring burden falls on them.

utterances.text: I haven't read the latest government report on methane monitoring, so I can't say how costly it is. What do you propose instead?

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: I'd say the tax would be unfair to small farms, because the measuring burden falls on them.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Methane from landfills is also a notable source of emissions.

utterances.speaker: Sipho

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: One practical detail is that the current collection day on my street is Tuesday.

utterances.text: Sipho, put another way, you doubt that the merger would cut administrative costs overall.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This policy is necessary because some pupils arrive at school too hungry to concentrate well.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that universal access to breakfast avoids marking some pupils as poor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The primary schools in my district renovated their kitchens last year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: School breakfast can help pupils begin the day ready to learn, which further supports this recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The case is stronger since providing breakfast at school can reduce the pressure on families during difficult mornings.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to adopt the policy is that a universal breakfast programme is simpler to administer than a programme that checks family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This recommendation is warranted because a free breakfast gives pupils a reliable opportunity to eat before lessons begin.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to adopt the policy is that offering breakfast to all pupils can improve attendance by making morning routines easier.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics raise one concern: funding free meals for well-off children would be an unjustified use of public money.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection is misplaced.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, public schools should make free breakfast a universal service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In plain terms, every pupil should be able to eat breakfast at school without paying or proving low family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To state the proposal once more, schools should offer breakfast free to all pupils.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether criminal records for minor offences should be automatically sealed after five crime-free years. Jelena, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: I do: criminal records for minor offences should be automatically sealed after five crime-free years because five crime-free years usually indicate that a person poses a low risk of repeating a minor offence.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Automatic sealing would improve employment prospects for people with minor convictions, which is a second reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: So you are saying that minor criminal records should automatically disappear after five crime-free years. But automatic sealing could prevent employers from seeing a pattern of repeated offending.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: I still support the policy, because automatic sealing would let people return to work without carrying a minor conviction forever.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal is a five-year clean-record rule for minor convictions.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: One more reason for automatic sealing is that many minor convictions result from one-time mistakes rather than persistent offending.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For offences outside the minor category, a review panel should handle sealing decisions. A review panel can distinguish a serious pattern of offending from an isolated lapse because a review panel should handle sealing decisions for offences outside the minor category.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Judges already have access to fuller case files that would help a review panel make those decisions. This is because a review panel should handle sealing decisions for offences outside the minor category, which makes the safeguard workable.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: So your safeguard is human review for offences that are not minor.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed review system would reserve panel decisions for more serious cases.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: For context, I have testified before parliamentary committees.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: The national criminal-record registry was launched in 2011.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays because those holidays require students to spend substantial time on worship and family observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I disagree: schools should keep homework deadlines during major religious holidays. The reason is that consistent deadlines prevent assignments from piling up afterward.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should require homework deadlines during major religious holidays. Many families plan their religious observances across several days, and that is another reason to adopt a ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students do not observe every major religious holiday.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Because schools should ban homework during major religious holidays, a homework ban would give students who observe religious holidays equal access to those holidays. Equal access to religious observance matters because it is part of fair treatment at school.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A short holiday exemption could replace a complete homework ban. It would preserve time for essential coursework, which is why I prefer the exemption.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, your exemption proposal would still permit assignments during the holiday. Permitting assignments would still pressure students to choose schoolwork over religious observance, and that is why I support a full ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A single national homework ban would be difficult to schedule. This difficulty is a reason to conclude that major religious holidays fall on different dates in different communities.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools can identify major religious holidays through published calendars, which makes a ban practical. In other words, published calendars allow schools to identify the holidays covered by the ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: To put your proposal another way, schools should suspend homework during major religious holidays. Put differently, one national ban would be hard to schedule across communities with different holiday dates.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays because those holidays require students to spend substantial time on worship and family observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I disagree: schools should keep homework deadlines during major religious holidays. The reason is that consistent deadlines prevent assignments from piling up afterward.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should require homework deadlines during major religious holidays. Many families plan their religious observances across several days, and that is another reason to adopt a ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students do not observe every major religious holiday. Several students also work part-time on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A homework ban would give students who observe religious holidays equal access to those holidays; this is another reason to adopt the ban. Equal access to religious observance matters because it is part of fair treatment at school.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A short holiday exemption could replace a complete homework ban. It would preserve time for essential coursework, which is why I prefer the exemption.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, your exemption proposal would still permit assignments during the holiday. Permitting assignments would still pressure students to choose schoolwork over religious observance, and that is why I support a full ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Major religious holidays fall on different dates in different communities. Because of that, a single national homework ban would be difficult to schedule.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools can identify major religious holidays through published calendars, which makes a ban practical. In other words, published calendars allow schools to identify the holidays covered by the ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: To put your proposal another way, schools should suspend homework during major religious holidays. Because of that proposal, one national ban would be hard to schedule across communities with different holiday dates.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should apartment buildings require residents to separate food waste from other rubbish? Joaquin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Yes, buildings should require it, since food waste makes up about a third of household rubbish by weight.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Rotting food in landfill also releases methane, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: And collected food waste can be turned into compost, which is one more reason for a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Constance, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But a mandate would be unenforceable in large buildings, since nobody can tell which flat put the wrong thing in a shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: So you are saying anonymous shared bins make fining residents impossible.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Yes. I live in a flat with a four-square-metre kitchen myself.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Fiona, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Cities with separate food collections cut contamination of recycling within a year, which is a reason to require it here.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Collection crews in those cities report visibly cleaner bags, which shows requiring separation pays off.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: So what you mean is that separate food collection makes recycling less contaminated.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kai, is there a middle way?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Rewards work better than fines, because residents ignore fines they believe cannot be traced to them.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A service-charge rebate for compliant buildings also costs less than policing, which is a further reason.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, carrots beat sticks.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Joaquin, can a requirement actually work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: A requirement can work in practice, because pilot buildings handed out free countertop caddies.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Participation also reached eighty percent in those pilots, which shows it works.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The city's collection trucks switched to electric last spring, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Separate food bins in the shared bin area are also usually collected on a different day from general rubbish in many cities.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should apartment buildings require residents to separate food waste from other rubbish? Joaquin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Yes, buildings should require it, since food waste makes up about a third of household rubbish by weight.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Rotting food in landfill also releases methane, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: And collected food waste can be turned into compost, which is one more reason for a requirement.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Constance, you are not convinced.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But a mandate would be unenforceable in large buildings, since nobody can tell which flat put the wrong thing in a shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: That is because anonymous shared bins make fining residents impossible.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Yes. I live in a flat with a four-square-metre kitchen myself.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Fiona, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Cities with separate food collections cut contamination of recycling within a year, which is a reason to require it here.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Collection crews in those cities report visibly cleaner bags, which shows requiring separation pays off.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: So what you mean is that separate food collection makes recycling less contaminated.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kai, is there a middle way?

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Rewards work better than fines, because residents ignore fines they believe cannot be traced to them.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: A service-charge rebate for compliant buildings also costs less than policing, which is a further reason.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, carrots beat sticks.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Joaquin, can a requirement actually work in practice?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: A requirement can work in practice, because pilot buildings handed out free countertop caddies.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Participation also reached eighty percent in those pilots, which shows it works.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The city's collection trucks switched to electric last spring, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether local councils should give tax discounts to shops that occupy vacant high-street premises. Milos, you support the proposal.

utterances.text: But tax discounts would reward landlords who leave premises empty instead of lowering rents. Separately, my council has twelve listed buildings.

utterances.speaker: Anders

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Eamon, what do local shopkeepers need most?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Independent retailers are more likely to sign short leases. The reason is that short leases let independent retailers test a new location.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: The panel has identified the potential benefit of filling empty units and the concern that discounts could subsidise landlords.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The central reason is that plurality voting can elect a legislator without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That happens because splitting votes among several candidates can allow a candidate opposed by most voters to win under plurality voting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Under ranked-choice voting, a voter's ballot transfers to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This gives voters a way to support a preferred candidate without wasting their vote if that candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: As a result, ranked-choice voting can produce a winner with support from voters whose first choices were eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a winner with support from transferred ballots has a broader mandate than a winner elected only through a plurality of first-choice votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics are right that replacing plurality voting could make elections confusing for voters, but that objection does not outweigh the democratic benefit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason for the concern is that voters may need to understand several preferences and the elimination process in a ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated. This is so because of that concern.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That process gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters; in other words, ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters, ranked-choice voting transfers a voter's ballot to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated; this is the same transfer rule described earlier.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Legislative elections determine who writes and votes on laws.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some voters prefer to read policy platforms before choosing a candidate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing election software can record and process ranked ballots, which is why ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The central reason is that plurality voting can elect a legislator without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That happens because splitting votes among several candidates can allow a candidate opposed by most voters to win under plurality voting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Under ranked-choice voting, a voter's ballot transfers to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This gives voters a way to support a preferred candidate without wasting their vote if that candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: As a result, ranked-choice voting can make the winning candidate more representative of the electorate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a winner with support from transferred ballots has a broader mandate than a winner elected only through a plurality of first-choice votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics are right that replacing plurality voting could make elections confusing for voters, but that objection does not outweigh the democratic benefit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason for the concern is that voters may need to understand several preferences and the elimination process in a ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That process gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters; in other words, ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters, ranked-choice voting transfers a voter's ballot to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated; this is the same transfer rule described earlier.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Legislative elections determine who writes and votes on laws.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some voters prefer to read policy platforms before choosing a candidate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing election software can record and process ranked ballots, which is why ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge patients who come in with non-urgent conditions. Amir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I say yes, they should charge, because non-urgent patients make up about a third of attendances and they lengthen waits for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Ayesha, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A charge would deter poor patients from coming in even when their condition is serious.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have worked as a hospital pharmacist for twenty years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge whether their condition is urgent, which is why a charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Collection systems in hospitals are expensive to run, as shown by the fact that charging would raise little money after the cost of collecting it.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Put another way, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge, since many people cannot get a same-day GP appointment. So the emergency department is all they have.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have worked as a triage nurse for twelve years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: A charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Charging would raise little money, but this is no surprise: collection systems in hospitals are expensive to run.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Separately, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge patients who come in with non-urgent conditions. Amir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I say yes, they should charge.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Ayesha, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A charge would deter poor patients from coming in even when their condition is serious.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge, since many people cannot get a same-day GP appointment. So the emergency department is all they have.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have not worked as a triage nurse for twelve years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge whether their condition is urgent, because a charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Charging would raise little money, but this is no surprise: hospital collection systems cost a lot to run.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Put another way, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge patients who come in with non-urgent conditions. Amir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I say yes, they should charge.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Ayesha, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A charge would deter poor patients from coming in even when their condition is serious.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge, since many people cannot get a same-day GP appointment. So the emergency department is all they have.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have worked as a triage nurse for twelve years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge whether their condition is urgent, which is why a charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Charging would raise little money, but this is no surprise: collection systems in hospitals are expensive to run.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Put another way, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: We will take a vote after the break.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Your council is debating whether to stock every public toilet with free period products. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Councils should provide free menstrual products in all public toilets, because so many people are caught out away from home without what they need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would it cost?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: It would cost less than one percent of the toilet maintenance budget, which is another reason to do it. I should say I chaired the equalities committee for three years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics worry about vandalism, though.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Critics say free dispensers get wrecked and emptied within days, but the neighbouring borough's year-long pilot lost almost no stock to vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the pilot's evidence shows that the cost of replacing vandalised stock is a negligible worry.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. And there is a further reason: teenage girls often miss school when they cannot afford these products.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should the men's toilets be included?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: They should, since trans men and non-binary people also menstruate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, every public toilet, whoever uses it.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Scotland has required free access since 2022, which shows that free provision works at national scale.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Food banks are reporting rising demand for these products, which is yet another reason the council should act.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Funny thing, my own daughter started her periods at eleven.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Separately, the council's public toilets are cleaned twice a day.

utterances.text: Critics worry about vandalism, though.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Critics say free dispensers get wrecked and emptied within days, but the neighbouring borough's year-long pilot lost almost no stock to vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the pilot's evidence shows the vandalism fear is unfounded.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. And there is a further reason: teenage girls often miss school when they cannot afford these products.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should the men's toilets be included?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: They should, since trans men and non-binary people also menstruate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The reason is that menstrual products should be available in every public toilet, whoever uses it.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Scotland has required free access since 2022, which shows that free provision works at national scale, and another reason it works is that menstrual products should be available in every public toilet, whoever uses it.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Food banks are reporting rising demand for these products, which is yet another reason the council should act.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Funny thing, my own daughter started her periods at eleven.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Your council is debating whether to stock every public toilet with free period products. Where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Councils should provide free menstrual products in all public toilets, because so many people are caught out away from home without what they need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would the cost to the council be?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: It would cost less than one percent of the toilet maintenance budget, which is another reason to do it. I should say I chaired the equalities committee for three years.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics worry about vandalism, though.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Critics say free dispensers get wrecked and emptied within days, but the neighbouring borough's year-long pilot lost almost no stock to vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the pilot's evidence shows the vandalism fear is unfounded.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. And there is a further reason: teenage girls often miss school when they cannot afford these products.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should the men's toilets be included?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: They should, since trans men and non-binary people also menstruate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, every public toilet, whoever uses it.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Scotland has required free access since 2022, which shows that free provision works at national scale.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Food banks are reporting rising demand for these products, which is yet another reason the council should act.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Funny thing, my own daughter started her periods at eleven.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Governments should tax vacant homes where housing is short, since thousands of homes in this city sit empty while families wait on housing lists.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: A tax would give owners a reason to rent out or sell, and that is how it would increase the supply of homes people can live in.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But many owners leave homes empty only because they are renovating or settling an estate, so a tax would punish them unfairly.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: My aunt waited two years for a probate decision on her late husband's house, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: The tax would only apply to homes empty for over twelve months without a legitimate reason, since we can write exemptions for renovation and probate into the tax.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: So you are saying the tax can be aimed at long-term speculative emptiness rather than ordinary owners.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Exactly, and in other words, owners respond to the incentive: Vancouver saw empty homes fall after its vacancy tax.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Anyway, I am off to a housing conference next month, so I will bring you the latest figures.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Next item: allowance versus paying for chores. Sipho, you start.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I think parents should give a fixed weekly allowance and not pay for chores. It lets children practise budgeting, since they know in advance how much they will have.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Paying per chore has a worse effect, because children learn to expect payment for every household task.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: That is why they end up refusing to help at home when they do not need money, which is a reason to prefer the flat allowance.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Right, and chores are a duty of living in a family, not a job, which is why payment for them is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Our neighbours saw this: their children stopped helping with the dishes once payment was introduced, which shows the problem is real.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But paying for chores teaches that money is earned through effort, so I doubt a fixed allowance is better.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: A flat allowance teaches that money arrives regardless of effort, which is why that objection has some force.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: In other words, children paid per chore will skip tasks whenever they have enough money.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Noted. By the way, the heating in this room goes off at five.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: At home we used a flat allowance with a short list of unpaid jobs.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: My children now manage their money well and still help at home, which supports that mix.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: So you are saying a flat allowance plus unpaid chores gives both budgeting practice and a sense of family duty.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Yes. Let us also write a short leaflet for parents summarising this.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should senior managers give a fixed share of their time to mentoring juniors? Zofia, you start.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Yes, a fixed ten percent of the week. Mentored juniors stay at the firm longer, and that is why I want it guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Why does staying longer matter so much?

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Since replacing a trained junior costs about half a year's salary, it matters a great deal.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: But a fixed quota would turn mentoring into box-ticking.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying managers would tick the box and the juniors would learn nothing.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Good mentors are chosen for their patience, not their rank. I started my career at a shipping firm in Gdansk, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Put another way, mentors should be picked for temperament rather than seniority. But that goes against the objection that a fixed quota would turn mentoring into box-ticking.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: My firm has forty senior managers, so I have watched this up close.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take your calls after the break.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether an independent commission, rather than legislators, should draw electoral boundaries. Jasper, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: An independent commission should draw the boundaries, because when legislators draw their own districts they get to choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But a commission answers to no voters, since its members are never elected.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Valentina, you have studied the commission states.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Commissions produce more competitive elections, since the share of uncompetitive districts fell by a third in states that adopted them. That is another reason to back Jasper's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Legislators should keep drawing the lines, because voters can throw them out after a bad map.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Camille, so you are saying commissions have no democratic legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: My own district is the size of a small county, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: But two commission maps were struck down by courts for splitting communities, which shows commissioners lack local knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, Isaac, you want the district lines kept in elected hands.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Competitiveness is not the right goal for a map, since a competitive map can still split a city.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying fair representation of communities matters more than competition.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: The state legislature redrew our map in a single weekend behind closed doors, which shows how legislators choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Voters should be able to remove whoever draws the maps: that is what accountability means.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: The next census is due in three years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether an independent commission, rather than legislators, should draw electoral boundaries. Jasper, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: An independent commission should draw the boundaries, because when legislators draw their own districts they get to choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But a commission answers to no voters, since its members are never elected.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Valentina, you have studied the commission states.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Commissions produce more competitive elections, since the share of uncompetitive districts fell by a third in states that adopted them. That is another reason to back Jasper's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Legislators should keep drawing the lines, because after a bad map voters have the power to throw them out.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Camille, so you are saying commissions have no democratic legitimacy?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: My own district is the size of a small county, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: But two commission maps were struck down by courts for splitting communities, which shows commissioners lack local knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, Isaac, you want the district lines kept in elected hands.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Competitiveness is not the right goal for a map. Separately, a competitive map can still split a city.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that fair representation of communities matters more than competition, Isaac?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: The state legislature redrew our map in a single weekend behind closed doors, which shows how legislators choose their voters.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, voters should be able to remove whoever draws the maps: that is what accountability means.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: The next census is due in three years.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether we should convert vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses. Petra, could you outline the practical case?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The council's procurement team meets on Thursday. Before that, I want us to settle the principle.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: The recommendation is that the local government should convert vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: I object to that recommendation, however: converting the vacant municipal buildings would expose the council to high renovation costs.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is for the local government to convert vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Since the council should make this conversion, unused public property would return to productive use.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Our committee has six voting members. Petra, what benefit would matter most to the businesses?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Because the council should make this conversion, small businesses would gain access to lower-cost premises.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Because the council should create these workspaces, the council would have a better chance of retaining local businesses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill, because a mandatory charge removes the diner's power to reward good service and penalise poor service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Without that power, servers have less incentive to try hard. And servers who try less hard give diners a worse experience.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I admit that many diners find tipping stressful and confusing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Automatic charges would spare diners the awkward arithmetic and social pressure of tipping.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But awkward arithmetic is a small price to pay for keeping control over what one pays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once ate at a seaside cafe where the bill carried a charge of twelve percent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, diners should be free to decide for themselves what a meal was worth.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a second problem: restaurants that add automatic charges keep their menu prices artificially low.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Low menu prices mislead diners about what a meal will actually cost, which is why the practice is a bad one.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants that add automatic charges mislead diners about the true cost of a meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some restaurants pool the charge and share it among kitchen staff as well as servers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pooling the charge is fairer to kitchen staff than leaving them with no share of tips.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a voluntary tip can still be pooled in just the same way.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My favourite waiter has worked at the same restaurant for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: So, to sum up, an optional, clearly suggested tip is the better compromise.

utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill, because a mandatory charge removes the diner's power to reward good service and penalise poor service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Without that power, servers have less incentive to try hard. And servers who try less hard give diners a worse experience.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I admit that many diners find tipping stressful and confusing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Automatic charges would spare diners the awkward arithmetic and social pressure of tipping.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But awkward arithmetic is a small price to pay for keeping control over what one pays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once ate at a seaside cafe where the bill carried a charge of twelve percent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, diners should be free to decide for themselves what a meal was worth.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a second problem: restaurants that add automatic charges keep their menu prices artificially low.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Low menu prices mislead diners about what a meal will actually cost, which shows that those restaurants keep their menu prices artificially low. That is why the practice is a bad one.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants that add automatic charges mislead diners about the true cost of a meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some restaurants pool the charge and share it among kitchen staff as well as servers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pooling the charge is fairer to kitchen staff than leaving them with no share of tips.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a voluntary tip can still be pooled in the same way.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My favourite waiter has worked at the same restaurant for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: So, to sum up, an optional, clearly suggested tip is the better compromise.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Welcome. Tonight we are asking whether routine antibiotic use in livestock should be prohibited entirely. Hollis, why should it remain available?

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Routine antibiotic use prevents some infections in crowded livestock barns. Because it prevents those infections, it lowers livestock deaths.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But routine antibiotic doses are often given to livestock that are not ill, so this is not simply treatment of disease.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: Repeated antibiotic exposure selects for resistant bacteria, and that makes some livestock infections harder to treat.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: In other words, resistance makes some infections harder to treat. Prohibiting routine antibiotic use would protect public health, which is why I support a complete prohibition.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Before we move on, several livestock producers have already changed their purchasing contracts.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: I still worry that a complete prohibition could leave farmers without a dependable way to prevent outbreaks.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: The debate will continue after tonight's broadcast.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Jin, resistance was your central concern. Because repeated exposure selects resistant bacteria, prohibiting routine antibiotic use would protect public health.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: That is why I think the policy should be adopted, although farms would need help improving hygiene and vaccination.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I think farmers should be banned from spraying organophosphates within 200 metres of schools and playgrounds. The reason is that children's developing bodies are more sensitive to these chemicals than adults' are.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Spray drift from the fields also regularly reaches playgrounds, which is a second reason.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But a 200-metre buffer would take a big share of the land from farmers with small plots right beside villages.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I grew up on a farm, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Wind-direction rules are enough, because spraying only when the wind blows away from buildings keeps drift off playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: So what you mean, Xavier, is that wind-direction rules alone would be enough.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Residues have turned up in playground dust 150 metres from sprayed fields, which shows drift really does reach children. Also, my cousin teaches at a primary school in the next county.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I could accept a buffer if the state compensated farmers, since the loss of land would fall on them alone.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: In other words, you would back the buffer provided the state pays farmers for the lost land.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I can live with that, since the state does not already pay crop subsidies and could not cover the compensation.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I think farmers should be banned from spraying organophosphates within 200 metres of schools and playgrounds. The reason is that children's developing bodies are more sensitive to these chemicals than adults' are.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Spray drift from the fields also regularly reaches playgrounds, which is a second reason.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But a 200-metre buffer would take a big share of the land from farmers with small plots right beside villages.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Wind-direction rules are enough, because spraying only when the wind blows away from buildings keeps drift off playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: So what you mean, Xavier, is that wind-direction rules alone would be enough.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Residues have turned up in playground dust 150 metres from sprayed fields, which shows drift really does reach children. Also, my cousin teaches at a primary school in the next county.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I could accept a buffer if the state compensated farmers, since the loss of land would fall on them alone.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: In other words, you would reject the buffer unless the state refused to pay farmers anything for the lost land, and even then only reluctantly.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I can live with that, since the state already pays crop subsidies and could cover the compensation.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should schools replace detention with restorative meetings after nonviolent misconduct? Fatima, you start.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, they should replace it, because detention teaches pupils nothing about the harm they caused. A child sits in silence for an hour and learns only to resent the clock.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Agnieszka, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: But detention keeps classrooms orderly, since pupils know exactly what follows a missed deadline. That predictability matters in a room of thirty.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Restorative meetings cut repeat offences, because a pupil who has to face the person they wronged feels responsible for it. That is why I back Fatima's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Saanvi, you are saying pupils alter their behaviour when they see what their actions did to others.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Meetings demand more staff time than schools can spare, because a single one takes about an hour of a trained facilitator's day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Agnieszka, the real obstacle is teacher workload.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Every detention session already requires a teacher to supervise it, so replacing it with meetings would cost little extra staff time. That is another reason to make the switch.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: I should say I ran a mediation club at my school for six years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Agnieszka, a last word before we close.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: By the way, I have taught geography for eleven years. I will leave it there.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should schools replace detention with restorative meetings after nonviolent misconduct? Fatima, you start.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, they should replace it, because detention teaches pupils very little about the harm they caused. A child sits in silence for an hour and learns only to resent the clock.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Agnieszka, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: But detention keeps classrooms orderly, since pupils know exactly what follows a missed deadline. That predictability matters in a room of thirty.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Restorative meetings cut repeat offences, because a pupil who has to face the person they wronged feels responsible for it. That is why I back Fatima's proposal.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Saanvi, you are saying pupils change when they see what their actions did to others.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Meetings demand more staff time than schools can spare, because a single one takes about an hour of a trained facilitator's day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Agnieszka, the real obstacle is teacher workload.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Detention already needs a teacher to supervise every session, so replacing it with meetings would cost little extra staff time. That is another reason to make the switch.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: I should say I ran a mediation club at my school for six years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Agnieszka, a last word before we close.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: By the way, I have taught geography for eleven years. I will leave it there.
