utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I think hospitals should not use AI to prioritise patients for scarce treatments, because an AI system applies the same criteria to every patient, whereas tired clinicians vary from one shift to the next.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: I accept what you said about the criteria, since AI ranking would be more consistent than ranking by clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: But an AI system would reproduce past inequalities in its rankings, since these tools are trained on historical records that reflect past under-diagnosis of some groups.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Quick aside: I work night shifts on a transplant ward, so I have seen how the variation plays out.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A hospital in the Netherlands audited its triage model every quarter and corrected the bias it found, which shows that regular audits can catch and correct bias in an AI triage model. That is a reason to support using AI for prioritisation.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Fair point. I would add that AI prioritisation is only acceptable if its rankings can be audited.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: I should say I have not actually seen the tool you both keep mentioning.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: In other words, the rankings would be open to audit, and that makes AI prioritisation acceptable.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Separately, waiting lists for elective surgery have grown in many countries over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I think hospitals should use AI to prioritise patients for scarce treatments, because an AI system applies the same criteria to every patient, whereas clinicians' decisions drift as they work long hours.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So you are saying that AI ranking would be more consistent than ranking by clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: But an AI system would reproduce past inequalities in its rankings, since these tools are trained on historical records that reflect past under-treatment of some groups.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Quick aside: I work night shifts on a transplant ward, so I have seen how the variation plays out.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A hospital in the Netherlands audited its triage model every quarter and corrected the bias it found, which shows that routine audits are able to detect and fix bias in an AI triage model. That is a reason to support using AI for prioritisation.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Fair point. I would add that AI prioritisation should only be introduced if the hospital publishes its rankings to the public.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: I should say I have not actually seen the tool you both keep mentioning.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Put another way, the rankings would be open to audit, and that makes AI prioritisation acceptable.

An AI system applies the same criteria to every patient, whereas clinicians' decisions drift as they work long hours.
Prioritisation by AI would be more consistent than prioritisation by clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Pregnant patients often cannot schedule antenatal appointments outside their working hours, and antenatal appointments can identify complications before they become emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That matters because unpaid time off for antenatal appointments can impose a financial penalty on pregnant patients.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers should offer pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment. However, some employers would find universal paid time off difficult to administer; that practical concern should not outweigh the case for this policy.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I keep my appointment reminders in a paper diary.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I would also include reasonable travel time, not just the consultation, in any paid entitlement.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That wider allowance is justified because waiting times at antenatal appointments can be unpredictable. It is also necessary since pregnant patients may have to travel a considerable distance to reach an antenatal clinic.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Because you are proposing paid time for the whole unavoidable journey and appointment, not merely the consultation, paid time off should cover reasonable travel time as well as the antenatal appointment itself.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes, and paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: In other words, Magnus means that every scheduled antenatal visit should qualify for paid time off. Put another way, Magnus is not limiting the entitlement to appointments that a manager considers medically important.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I think the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory entitlement could create an administrative burden for small employers, but that burden is not a reason to reject legal protection. The entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law. Because that entitlement should be protected by law, a clear legal rule would give employers and pregnant patients consistent expectations.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers should also allow pregnant patients some flexibility in choosing appointment times.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That is practical because flexible scheduling can reduce disruption to colleagues and services.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The clinic near my home has green chairs in its waiting room.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Pregnant patients often cannot schedule antenatal appointments outside their working hours, and antenatal appointments can identify complications before they become emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That matters because unpaid time off for antenatal appointments can impose a financial penalty on pregnant patients.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Some employers would find universal paid time off difficult to administer. Even so, those practical concerns should not outweigh the case for employers offering pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I would also include reasonable travel time, not just the consultation, in any paid entitlement.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That wider allowance is justified because antenatal appointments can involve unpredictable waiting times. It is also necessary since pregnant patients may have to travel a considerable distance to reach an antenatal clinic.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: So you are proposing paid time for the whole unavoidable journey and appointment, not merely the consultation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes, and paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: In other words, Magnus means that every scheduled antenatal visit should qualify for paid time off. Put another way, Magnus is not limiting the entitlement to appointments that a manager considers medically important.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I think the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory entitlement could create an administrative burden for small employers, but that burden is not a reason to reject legal protection. A clear legal rule would give employers and pregnant patients consistent expectations.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers should give pregnant patients some choice over when they attend appointments.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That is practical because flexible scheduling can reduce disruption to colleagues and services.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The clinic near my home has green chairs in its waiting room.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Pregnant patients often cannot schedule antenatal appointments outside their working hours, and antenatal appointments can identify complications before they become emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That matters because unpaid time off for antenatal appointments can impose a financial penalty on pregnant patients.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Some employers would find universal paid time off difficult to administer. Even so, those practical concerns should not outweigh the case for employers offering pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I keep my appointment reminders in a paper diary.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I would also include reasonable travel time, not just the consultation, in any paid entitlement.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That wider allowance is justified because antenatal appointments can involve unpredictable waiting times. It is also necessary since pregnant patients may have to travel a considerable distance to reach an antenatal clinic.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So you are proposing paid time for the whole unavoidable journey and appointment, not merely the consultation.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Yes, and paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: In other words, Magnus means that every scheduled antenatal visit should qualify for paid time off. Put another way, Magnus is not limiting the entitlement to appointments that a manager considers medically important.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I think the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A statutory entitlement could create an administrative burden for small employers, but that burden is not a reason to reject legal protection. A clear legal rule would give employers and pregnant patients consistent expectations.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Employers should also allow pregnant patients some flexibility in choosing appointment times.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That is practical because flexible scheduling can reduce disruption to colleagues and services.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: The clinic near my home has green chairs in its waiting room.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether students should be allowed to retake failed exams without their original grades counting. Karima, would you begin?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A failed first attempt can depress a student's academic record even after the student later masters the material. That is why a retake without the original grade counting would measure the student's current competence more fairly.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Before we decide, note that the registrar closes the examination-entry system at five o'clock on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: For that reason, I support allowing the retake without the original grade counting. A shared retake rule would give all departments comparable records, which is another reason to adopt the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A second attempt can show whether a student has learned from feedback on the failed exam. Because of that, the retake process should require students to review the feedback before taking the exam again.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: An original failing grade can help advisers identify students who need academic support. Therefore, advisers should still be able to see that grade even if it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Keeping the original grade visible would help employers interpret a student's transcript. It follows that the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A common rubric for recording retakes would make transcripts easier to interpret. That is another reason to retain the original grade as a visible but non-counting entry.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying that a common rubric would standardize how retakes appear in student records?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a retake without the original grade would measure present competence rather than past failure.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: I have a concern, however: removing the original grade entirely could make it harder to detect repeated academic difficulties. That objection means I cannot support deleting the grade from every record.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: As a separate administrative note, the student union has scheduled its next general meeting for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: But the claim that the original grade would help employers is not persuasive because employers rarely receive detailed university transcripts. I would not use that point to justify keeping the grade visible.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, the retake process would require students to review feedback before making another attempt.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, advisers would retain access to the original failing grade without using it in the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Because the transcript would show the original grade without allowing that grade to affect the final mark, the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark. We will draft a policy reflecting that distinction.

utterances.text: Keeping the original grade visible would help employers interpret a student's transcript. It follows that the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A common rubric for recording retakes would make transcripts easier to interpret. That is another reason to retain the original grade as a visible but non-counting entry.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying that a common rubric would standardize how retakes appear in student records?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a retake without the original grade would measure present competence rather than past failure.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: I have a concern, however: removing the original grade entirely could make it harder to detect repeated academic difficulties. That objection means I cannot support deleting the grade from every record.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: As a separate administrative note, the student union has scheduled its next general meeting for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: But the claim that the original grade would help employers is not persuasive because employers rarely receive detailed university transcripts. I would not use that point to justify keeping the grade visible.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, the retake process would require students to review feedback before making another attempt.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, advisers would retain access to the original failing grade without using it in the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The university's retake policy will be printed in the student handbook.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: To sum up, the transcript would show the original grade without allowing that grade to affect the final mark. We will draft a policy reflecting that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: The examination office will archive the retake records digitally.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether students should be allowed to retake failed exams without their original grades counting. Karima, would you begin?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A failed first attempt can depress a student's academic record even after the student later masters the material. That is why a retake without the original grade counting would measure the student's current competence more fairly.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Before we decide, note that the registrar closes the examination-entry system at five o'clock on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: For that reason, I support allowing the retake without the original grade counting. A shared retake rule would give all departments comparable records, which is another reason to adopt the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A second attempt can show whether a student has learned from feedback on the failed exam. Because of that, the retake process should require students to review the feedback before taking the exam again.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: An original failing grade can help advisers identify students who need academic support. Therefore, advisers should be able to consult the original failing grade as background information, while it remains excluded from the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Keeping the original grade visible would help employers interpret a student's transcript. It follows that the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A common rubric for recording retakes would standardize how retakes appear in student records. That is another reason to retain the original grade as a visible but non-counting entry.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying that a common rubric would standardize how retakes appear in student records?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Exactly. In other words, a retake without the original grade would measure present competence rather than past failure.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: I have a concern, however: removing the original grade entirely could make it harder to detect repeated academic difficulties. That objection means I cannot support deleting the grade from every record.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: As a separate administrative note, the student union has scheduled its next general meeting for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: But the claim that the original grade would help employers is not persuasive because employers rarely receive detailed university transcripts. I would not use that point to justify keeping the grade visible.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, the retake process would require students to review feedback before making another attempt.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, advisers would retain access to the original failing grade without using it in the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: To sum up, the transcript would show the original grade without allowing that grade to affect the final mark. We will draft a policy reflecting that distinction.

utterances.text: A failed first attempt can depress a student's academic record even after the student later masters the material. That is why a retake without the original grade counting would measure the student's current competence more fairly.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Before we decide, note that the registrar closes the examination-entry system at five o'clock on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: For that reason, I support allowing the retake without the original grade counting. A shared retake rule would give all departments comparable records, which is another reason to adopt the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A second attempt can show whether a student has learned from feedback on the failed exam. Because of that, the retake process should require students to review the feedback before taking the exam again.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: An original failing grade can help advisers identify students who need academic support. Therefore, advisers should still be able to see that grade even if it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Keeping the original grade visible would help employers interpret a student's transcript. It follows that the original grade should remain visible on the transcript even when it does not count toward the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A common rubric for recording retakes would make transcripts easier to interpret. That is another reason to retain the original grade as a visible but non-counting entry.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: So you are saying that a common rubric would standardize how retakes appear in student records?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Exactly. Because Karima is saying that a retake without the original grade would not measure present competence rather than past failure, a retake without the original grade counting would measure a student's current competence more fairly.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: I have a concern, however: removing the original grade entirely could make it harder to detect repeated academic difficulties. That objection means I cannot support deleting the grade from every record.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: As a separate administrative note, the student union has scheduled its next general meeting for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: But the claim that the original grade would help employers is not persuasive because employers rarely receive detailed university transcripts. I would not use that point to justify keeping the grade visible.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, the retake process would require students to review feedback before making another attempt.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: In other words, advisers would retain access to the original failing grade without using it in the final mark.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: To sum up, the transcript would show the original grade without allowing that grade to affect the final mark. We will draft a policy reflecting that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should a company repay professional exam fees only if the employee stays on for a set period? Bilal, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Companies should require a two-year stay after paying exam fees, since otherwise they end up funding training for their competitors.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But repayment clauses damage morale, because employees who feel unable to leave stop making an effort.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a view on this.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Before we go on, a note on timing: most professional exam courses run for between six months and two years.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Training fees are an investment, and that is why a stay requirement is reasonable. I should say I sat my own accountancy exams ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Put another way, a firm is entitled to see its money put to work.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That ignores that firms gain from better-qualified staff whether or not they leave, since the new skills show up in daily work.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying the company is already repaid through better work.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A pro-rata clause is the fair middle ground. Besides, small firms simply cannot absorb the departure of a newly qualified employee.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Pro-rata is better, I will grant, because it lets people leave without crippling debt.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: A third of newly certified staff leave within a year, which is why firms need a stay requirement.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: But that figure comes from the financial sector, which is not typical.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Lars, what you mean is that you want a pro-rata clause as a middle path between full repayment and none.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: My own employer paid for my certificate and never asked for anything back.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: One more practical point: some exam bodies set their own fee schedules, which differ widely from year to year.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Whatever we choose, contracts should state the repayment terms before the course begins, since employees cannot judge the size of the commitment otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should a company repay professional exam fees only if the employee stays on for a set period? Bilal, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Companies should require a two-year stay after paying exam fees, since otherwise they end up funding training for their competitors.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But repayment clauses damage morale, because employees who feel unable to leave stop making an effort.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a view on this.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Training fees are an investment, and that is why a stay requirement is reasonable. I should say I sat my own accountancy exams ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, a firm is entitled to see its money put to work.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That ignores that firms gain from better-qualified staff whether or not they leave, since the new skills show up in daily work.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying the company is already repaid through better work.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: A pro-rata clause is the fair middle ground. Besides, small firms simply cannot absorb the departure of a newly qualified employee.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Pro-rata is better, I will grant, because it lets people leave without crippling debt.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A third of newly certified staff leave within a year, which is why firms need a stay requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: But that figure comes from the financial sector, which is not typical.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Lars, what you mean is that you want a pro-rata clause as a middle path between full repayment and none.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: My own employer paid for my certificate and never asked for anything back.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Whatever we choose, contracts should state the repayment terms before the course begins, since employees cannot judge the size of the commitment otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Film studios have used computer-generated imagery for decades.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A convincing fake video can spread to millions of viewers before anyone checks it, since creators should be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A separate reason to require watermarks is that viewers cannot reliably tell synthetic footage from the real thing by eye. In other words, without a visible mark, ordinary viewers cannot judge whether a realistic video is synthetic.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But watermarks can be cropped out or removed with editing tools.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That objection ignores that invisible watermarks embedded in the file data survive cropping and re-encoding in most tests, which is why removal is harder than it sounds.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A watermark rule would also punish honest creators while malicious actors simply ignore it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Honest creators already label their work voluntarily, so the rule would mainly give platforms a clear standard for removing unlabelled fakes. Put another way, a labelling rule gives platforms a clear standard for removing unlabelled fakes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I should say that I edit a small gardening channel.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Several countries have started drafting rules on labelling AI-generated media.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put simply, requiring watermarks protects public trust in video evidence.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters because courts and newsrooms have lately begun to ask for proof of origin for submitted footage.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Video platforms host far more footage today than they did a decade ago.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I think parents should be allowed to choose embryos with increased resistance to disease, because it spares children lifelong suffering.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Children with stronger resistance spend far less time in hospital, and that is the reason it spares them suffering.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Selection also does not only pick among embryos that already exist, since it edits embryos too, which is another reason to allow it.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I should say I have followed this field closely since my daughter was born.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Some object, though, that selection could widen the gap between rich and poor families.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Clinics already screen embryos for some inherited conditions.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Embryo screening for disease resistance is currently available in only a handful of countries.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: In other words, families should be free to pick the healthier embryo.

utterances.speaker: Hector

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether blood donors should receive small financial payments rather than only refreshments and recognition. Naveen, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: The region's blood supply has fallen below its usual winter reserve. Small payments would attract occasional blood donors, and that is the reason I support offering them.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Before we decide, note that the meeting room's projector was replaced on Monday.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: For that reason, I suggest that the committee should offer small financial payments to blood donors.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: However, small financial payments could crowd out donors who give blood from altruistic motives. A recent donor survey found that many regular donors value the current recognition more than monetary rewards, which is why that concern deserves attention.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal is to give blood donors modest payments in addition to recognition and refreshments.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The blood service would face only a small administrative cost for administering modest donor payments.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Payments could improve donor retention by giving occasional donors an additional reason to return.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Taken together, the proposed policy, its small administrative cost, and its possible retention benefit show that the committee should recommend modest payments because the policy could attract occasional donors, impose only a small administrative cost, and improve donor retention.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: In other words, the recommendation is for the committee to introduce modest payments alongside refreshments and recognition for blood donors.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether annual bonuses should depend more on team performance than on individual targets. Gideon, you support a change?

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Yes. Employees' results often depend on contributions from their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Laleh, what follows from that principle?

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team-weighted bonuses better reflect shared responsibility for results; therefore, employees' results often depend on contributions from their colleagues. Because employees' results often depend on colleagues, individual targets can unfairly penalize employees for problems caused by colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: For that reason, team performance measures would encourage employees to help across departmental boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: A team-based bonus would also reduce arguments about who deserves credit for joint work, because employees' results often depend on contributions from their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Because employees' results are interconnected, annual bonuses should therefore give more weight to team performance than to individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Because employees' results often depend on colleagues' work, team targets would make cooperation a visible part of performance assessment.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: That same dependence is why a greater team component would make the bonus system fairer for employees whose work is interdependent.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Employees' results often depend on what their colleagues contribute; therefore, employees' results often depend on contributions from their colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Put another way, employees' results are frequently tied to their colleagues' contributions.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: To sum up, employees' results commonly depend on contributions from other employees.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: But individual performance can still be assessed fairly even when employees depend on colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: We have heard the main arguments. Femi, one final comment before we close.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: The programme is being recorded for the station's archive.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will leave the final decision to the company's board.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments cap the fees payment processors charge small businesses? Pradeep, you start.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Small shops pay around three percent on every card sale, which is a large share of their thin profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Olumide, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: And they cannot bargain, since small businesses have no power to negotiate fees with the processors.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a cap would make small merchants worse off, because it would push processors to drop the smallest merchants or cut services such as fraud protection.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I should say I used to own a bakery, so I have seen those statements first hand.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Processors will leave small businesses without services, which is why a cap is a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Petra, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Not really. Processors already compete for small merchants, and fees have fallen by a fifth in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small merchants are weak in bargaining and cannot compare offers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are running ten minutes over, so briefly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Petra, your point that processors already compete for small merchants holds because competition among processors is already keeping fees down.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, small merchants lack the bargaining power to negotiate fees.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: No, I mean a cap is justified only if processors are unconstrained, and they are not.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Fee caps in other countries have caused processors to withdraw from small merchants.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Card payments now account for most retail purchases in many cities.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments cap the fees payment processors charge small businesses? Pradeep, you start.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Small shops pay around three percent on every card sale, which is a large share of their thin profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Olumide, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: And they cannot bargain, since small businesses have no power to negotiate fees with the processors.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a cap would make small merchants worse off, because it would push processors to drop the smallest merchants or cut services such as fraud protection.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I should say I used to own a bakery, so I have seen those statements first hand myself.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Processors will leave small businesses without services, which is why a cap is a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Petra, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Not really. Processors already compete for small merchants, and fees have fallen by a fifth in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small merchants are weak in bargaining and cannot compare offers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are running ten minutes over, so briefly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Petra, you are saying competition among processors is already keeping fees down.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, small merchants lack the bargaining power to negotiate fees.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: No, I mean a cap is justified only if processors are unconstrained, and they are not.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Fee caps in other countries have not caused processors to withdraw from small merchants.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should sixteen-year-olds be allowed to vote in local elections?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote in local elections. The reason is that voting at sixteen would give young people practical experience of civic participation.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Did your own experience influence that view?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I first attended a local council meeting at seventeen.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest argument against your proposal?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Some sixteen-year-olds lack enough knowledge to make informed local voting decisions. That objection is understandable, but it should not decide the issue.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that sixteen-year-olds should be required to vote in local elections?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Exactly. Many sixteen-year-olds already follow local issues.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The next local election will take place in May.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: In other words, voting at sixteen would give young people practical experience of civic participation; those existing habits support that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: A council survey found that it is not the case that sixteen-year-olds often follow local issues but sometimes misunderstand ballot procedures. That finding supports the point that many already follow local issues and, because it also shows confusion, supports the concern about their voting knowledge.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether councils ought to compel landlords to fit basic energy-saving measures before a rental licence can be renewed. Priya, please open.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Councils should require it, because tenants in poorly insulated homes pay hundreds of pounds more a year on heating.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: But landlords will simply pass the cost on through higher rents. I should say I let out a flat myself.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, in other words, tenants would end up footing the bill anyway.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Basic measures would add very little to rents, since loft insulation and draught-proofing cost a landlord only a few hundred pounds; that is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Emeka, you have doubts of a different kind?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Enforcement is the real problem, because our council has two inspectors for 9,000 licensed homes.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Put another way, Emeka, the rule would exist on paper only.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Then licence fees should pay for more inspectors, since each renewal already brings in a fee.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying, Priya, that landlords' own fees should pay for the inspections.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Possibly, though my own council has just cut its housing budget.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question is whether governments should automatically register every citizen who is eligible to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote, because electoral offices already receive reliable information about many citizens' eligibility from public records.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: But automatic registration would expose citizens to errors in identity or eligibility records.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Automatic registration would increase voter participation, because it would eliminate an application step that keeps some eligible citizens off the electoral roll.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: The registration office in my county opens for only four hours on Fridays. That makes the current process especially inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The proposed system would place eligible citizens on electoral rolls automatically.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: But that participation benefit is not guaranteed: automatic registration would not guarantee higher voter turnout.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposal would put eligible citizens on the electoral rolls without requiring them to submit an application?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Yes, and automatic registration would protect eligible citizens from administrative barriers because individual registration requires citizens to navigate deadlines and forms.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Put another way, eligible citizens would face fewer administrative obstacles under automatic registration.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: I have voted in every national election since turning eighteen, so my own experience is not typical of people who are missed by the system.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: What group would benefit most from automatic registration?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Automatic registration would reach citizens who frequently change address, because citizens who frequently change address are more likely to miss registration deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: That conclusion has another reason: citizens who move often are disproportionately likely to miss registration deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Before any launch, the public registry must be audited, since outdated addresses could create duplicate or inaccurate voter records.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: To state that safeguard plainly, automatic registration should follow an audit of the public registry.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would raise voter participation.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question is whether governments should automatically register every citizen who is eligible to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote, because electoral offices already receive reliable information about many citizens' eligibility from public records.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: But automatic registration would expose citizens to errors in identity or eligibility records.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Automatic registration would increase voter participation, because it would remove an application step that prevents some eligible citizens from appearing on the electoral roll.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: The registration office in my county opens for only four hours on Fridays. That makes the current process especially inconvenient.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The proposed system would place eligible citizens on electoral rolls automatically.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: But that participation benefit is not guaranteed: automatic registration would not guarantee higher voter turnout.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: So you are saying the proposal would put eligible citizens on the electoral rolls without requiring them to submit an application?

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Yes, and automatic registration would protect eligible citizens from administrative barriers because individual registration requires citizens to navigate deadlines and forms.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Put another way, eligible citizens would face fewer administrative obstacles under automatic registration.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: What group would benefit most from automatic registration?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Automatic registration would reach citizens who frequently change address, because citizens who frequently change address are more likely to miss registration deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: That conclusion has another reason: citizens who move often are disproportionately likely to miss registration deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Before any launch, the public registry must be audited, since outdated addresses could create duplicate or inaccurate voter records.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration should not begin until officials have verified the public registry's accuracy.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would raise voter participation, which shows that a public registry must be audited before automatic registration begins.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I think restorative-justice conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences. I should say I'm only a volunteer facilitator, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But dropping prosecution would take away the deterrent for other teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That ignores that teenagers rarely weigh penalties before acting, since their impulse control is still developing.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So you are saying deterrence simply does not work on teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Exactly, and conferences cut reoffending, because a local pilot recorded 25 percent reoffending against 40 percent after court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But young offenders could end up feeling coerced into pardoning, since some victims in other schemes say they felt obliged to accept an apology.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Victims choose whether to attend; in other words, nobody is forced to meet the offender.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So what you mean is the choice sits with the victim.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Offenders must admit guilt first, so no innocent juvenile would be pushed through, which is another reason to replace prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Repeat offenders need prosecution, since conferences cannot compel any supervision.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, repeat offenders would stay with the courts, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew went through a school mediation last year.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I think restorative-justice conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences. I should say I'm only a volunteer facilitator, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But dropping prosecution would take away the deterrent for other teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That ignores that teenagers rarely weigh penalties before acting, since their impulse control is still developing.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So you are saying deterrence simply does not work on teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Exactly, and conferences cut reoffending, because a local pilot recorded 25 percent reoffending against 40 percent after court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But victims may be pressured into forgiving, since some victims in other schemes say they felt obliged to accept an apology.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Victims choose whether to attend; in other words, nobody is forced to meet the offender.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So what you mean is the choice sits with the victim.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Offenders must admit guilt first, so no innocent juvenile would be pushed through, which is another reason to replace prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Repeat offenders need prosecution, since conferences cannot compel any supervision.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, repeat offenders would stay with the courts, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew went through a school mediation last year.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Separately, juvenile offences are recorded differently in each district.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I think restorative-justice conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences. I should say I'm only a volunteer facilitator, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But dropping prosecution would take away the deterrent for other teenagers.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That ignores that teenagers rarely weigh penalties before acting, since their impulse control is still developing.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So you are saying deterrence simply does not work on teenagers.

utterances.text: Exactly, and conferences cut reoffending, because a local pilot recorded 25 percent reoffending against 40 percent after court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But some victims in other schemes say they felt obliged to accept an apology, since victims may be pressured into forgiving.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Victims choose whether to attend; in other words, nobody is forced to meet the offender.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: So what you mean is the choice sits with the victim.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Offenders must admit guilt first, so no innocent juvenile would be pushed through, which is another reason to replace prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Repeat offenders need prosecution, since conferences cannot compel any supervision.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put another way, repeat offenders would stay with the courts, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew went through a school mediation last year.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support that proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. I support that policy because demographic representation affects whether treatment safety is properly assessed.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But equal demographic quotas can make trial samples less representative of patients in actual practice.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: The reason I still favor the requirement is that, without equal representation, a treatment can appear safe for one group while harming another. I served on a hospital research committee last spring.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To put Nkechi's position another way, clinical trials should have equal enrollment from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Equal enrollment makes comparisons between demographic subgroups more reliable, which is why the requirement is justified. Requiring equal enrollment also forces researchers to test whether results hold across demographic groups, and that is another reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy is a requirement for equal enrollment across all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Exactly; the proposal requires clinical trials to enroll equal numbers from every major demographic group.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, the policy would require equal demographic representation in clinical trials. Equal enrollment would also make important differences in treatment response harder to overlook, which is another reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The requirement is also justified because equal demographic enrollment would improve public confidence in clinical-trial evidence. A final reason is that equal enrollment would reduce the risk that medical guidelines are based mainly on evidence from one population.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support that proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. I support that policy because demographic representation affects whether treatment safety is properly assessed.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But unequal demographic enrollment can make trial samples less representative of patients in actual practice. I have reviewed clinical-trial protocols for several years.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: The reason I still favor the requirement is that, without equal representation, a treatment can appear safe for one group while harming another. I served on a hospital research committee last spring.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To restate Nkechi's position, clinical trials should enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Equal enrollment makes comparisons between demographic subgroups more reliable, which is why the requirement is justified. Requiring equal enrollment also forces researchers to test whether results hold across demographic groups, and that is another reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the policy is a requirement for equal enrollment across all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Exactly; the proposal requires clinical trials to enroll equal numbers from every major demographic group.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, the policy would require equal demographic representation in clinical trials. Equal enrollment would also make important differences in treatment response harder to overlook, which is another reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Clinical trials may use different methods for collecting participant data.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The requirement is also justified because equal demographic enrollment would improve public confidence in clinical-trial evidence. A final reason is that equal enrollment would reduce the risk that medical guidelines are based mainly on evidence from one population.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Some clinical trials recruit participants at multiple research sites.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should health insurers cover weight-loss medications for people who do not have diabetes? Gabriela, you first.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Yes, insurers should cover them, because obesity drives heart disease, stroke and joint problems.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Early treatment lowers later hospital costs, which is another reason to cover them. And trials show patients lose about fifteen percent of their body weight, which shows the drugs deliver.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying insurers ought to pay for these drugs for patients without diabetes. Harriet?

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: But these drugs cost over a thousand dollars a month. That also ignores that patients regain most of the weight once they stop taking them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jolene, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Coverage should be limited to people with a BMI above 35, because without a limit premiums would rise for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: In other words, only people with severe obesity should be covered.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Yes. The drugs are most cost-effective in severe obesity, which is why a cutoff makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Put another way, insurers would pay only for the severe cases. Incidentally, the first of these drugs was approved for obesity in 2021.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments build desalination plants despite the energy use and marine impacts? Wilhelmina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because coastal cities cannot rely on rainfall alone as droughts grow longer and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, what is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Desalination gives a supply that does not depend on rainfall, in other words a source that works through a drought.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: These plants burn enormous amounts of electricity, which is why they are too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tariq?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But solar and wind farms built alongside them can power the plants, so the plants' operating costs will fall below those of conventional water treatment.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, a personal note?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: I have lived in a drought-hit town for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And the marine side?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Brine discharge raises salinity near outfalls and harms seabed life.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: That marine damage is a serious cost, since the brine harms the seabed.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Diffusers spreading brine over a wide area dilute it quickly, which is a reason to doubt how serious the damage is.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, alternatives?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Fixing leaking pipes would save more water than a new plant, because marine damage is a serious cost.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Let me sum up Gareth: so you are saying desalination is too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice, given huge electricity use.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And Wilhelmina, so you are saying dry cities need a supply independent of rainfall.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: The pipe-fixing programme in the region began last year.

props.text: Governments should build desalination plants despite their energy use and marine impacts.
Coastal cities cannot rely on rainfall alone, because droughts are becoming longer and more frequent.
Desalination gives a water supply that does not depend on rainfall.
Desalination plants use enormous amounts of electricity.
Desalination is too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice.
Plants can be powered by solar and wind farms built alongside them.
The operating costs of desalination plants powered by solar and wind will fall below those of conventional water treatment.
Gareth has lived in a drought-hit town for ten years.
Brine discharge raises salinity near outfalls and harms seabed life.
Marine damage from desalination is a serious cost.
Diffusers that spread brine over a wide area dilute it quickly.
Fixing leaking pipes would save more water than a new plant would produce.
Desalination is too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice, in Gareth's words, because of its huge electricity use.
Wilhelmina's view is that dry cities need a supply independent of rainfall.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because without caps the richest clubs buy the best players and win almost every title.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, your response?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: And competitive balance is what keeps fans interested, which is another reason. Small clubs in uncapped leagues are also forced to sell their best young players.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But caps would hold down players' wages unfairly, since players have a short career and deserve to earn whatever the market offers.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Rafael, is that wealthy clubs win nearly every title.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Look at the American leagues: caps there have produced a much wider spread of champions than European leagues without caps. And players' unions in capped leagues negotiated guaranteed minimum shares of revenue.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Which shows that caps do not squeeze players' wages unfairly, contrary to what Ivana says.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Rich clubs still spend on coaching, facilities and scouting, so capped leagues still see them dominate, and that ignores your American example.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I play amateur football on Sundays, so I have seen the budgets up close.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, summarise.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Wealth finds a way around the cap, in other words, the cap fails. Enforcement needs an independent auditor with real powers, since caps with no enforcement are worthless because clubs conceal payments through side deals.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rafael, last thoughts?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Pair the cap with revenue sharing, because revenue sharing narrows the gap between big and small clubs more directly. In other words, enforcement matters most.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: One more fact?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Some national federations already publish the salary figures of their professional clubs each season.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Broadcast rights revenue is rising faster than ticket revenue.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national sports federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because without caps the richest clubs buy the best players and win almost every title.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, your response?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: And competitive balance is what keeps fans interested, which is another reason. Small clubs in uncapped leagues are also forced to sell their best young players.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana?

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But caps would hold down players' wages unfairly, since players have a short career and deserve to earn whatever the market offers.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Rafael, is that wealthy clubs win nearly every title.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Look at the American leagues: caps there have produced a much wider spread of champions than European leagues without caps. And players' unions in capped leagues negotiated guaranteed minimum shares of revenue.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Which shows that caps do not squeeze players' wages unfairly, contrary to what Ivana says.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Rich clubs still spend on coaching, facilities and scouting, so capped leagues still see them dominate, and that ignores your American example.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I play amateur football on Sundays, so I have seen the budgets up close.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, summarise.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Wealth finds a way around the cap, so the cap fails, and that is why capped leagues still see rich clubs dominate through non-salary spending. Enforcement needs an independent auditor with real powers, since caps without enforcement are worthless because clubs hide payments through side deals.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rafael, last thoughts?

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Pair the cap with revenue sharing, because revenue sharing narrows the gap between big and small clubs more directly. In other words, enforcement matters most.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: One more fact?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Broadcast rights revenue is rising faster than ticket revenue.

utterances.speaker: Ivana

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, summarise.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether online voting should be introduced for national elections. Alina, you start.

utterances.text: Online voting should be introduced for national elections, because turnout among young and mobile voters would rise.

utterances.text: Fatima, do you see other benefits?

utterances.text: Yes, since it would make voting accessible to disabled people who struggle to reach polling stations, it is another reason to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: I agree that online voting would make voting accessible to disabled people who struggle to reach polling stations, because my neighbour once waited two hours at a polling station.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: I disagree, because online voting systems cannot be made secure enough for national elections, which is why hackers could alter votes without anyone noticing.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: But Estonia has run online voting for many years without proven tampering.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Astrid, the reason hackers could alter votes without anyone noticing is that online voting would let hostile actors alter results unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will return after the break.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets. Noor, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Urban neighborhoods with little tree canopy become hotter in summer. Because of that, new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I oppose mandatory tree-canopy targets because they would raise construction costs. My apartment overlooks a busy bus depot, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Tree canopy absorbs rain during storms, and that is why retaining trees can reduce the size of new drainage systems.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: So you are saying that trees can handle some stormwater before it reaches underground pipes.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Exactly, and that is why smaller drainage systems can reduce the infrastructure cost of a development.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Lower infrastructure costs can offset part of the expense of meeting canopy targets, which shows that long-term public savings make a strong case for requiring tree canopy in new developments.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Trees shade streets and buildings, so tree canopy can reduce the heat experienced by residents of new developments.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, tree canopy can make new neighborhoods cooler for their residents.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: But canopy requirements can be met without making new homes unaffordable. Flexible site designs can keep the cost of meeting canopy requirements manageable, because builders can place trees alongside rather than underneath every structure.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Given those long-term public savings, flexible canopy targets can be affordable when those savings are counted. In other words, affordable flexible targets can preserve meaningful tree canopy, because flexible site designs can keep the cost of meeting canopy requirements manageable.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: For context, my local council planted twelve thousand trees last year.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: To put Malik's economic point another way, public savings are an important justification for requiring canopy in new developments.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets. Noor, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: New housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I oppose mandatory tree-canopy targets because they would raise construction costs. My apartment overlooks a busy bus depot, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Tree canopy absorbs rain during storms, and that is why retaining trees can reduce the size of new drainage systems.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: So you are saying that trees can handle some stormwater before it reaches underground pipes.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Exactly, and that is why smaller drainage systems can reduce the infrastructure cost of a development.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Lower infrastructure costs can offset part of the expense of meeting canopy targets, which shows that long-term public savings make a strong case for requiring tree canopy in new developments.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Trees shade streets and buildings, so residents of new developments can experience less heat because of tree canopy.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, tree canopy can make new neighborhoods cooler for their residents.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: But canopy requirements can be satisfied without pricing new homes beyond what buyers can afford. Flexible site designs can keep the cost of meeting canopy requirements manageable, because builders can place trees alongside rather than underneath every structure.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Given those long-term public savings, flexible canopy targets can be affordable when those savings are counted. In other words, affordable flexible targets can preserve meaningful tree canopy.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: To put Malik's economic point another way, public savings are an important justification for requiring canopy in new developments.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Parties should face strict limits on total campaign spending, because if spending is left uncapped, the parties backed by rich donors can easily overwhelm their rivals.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Why would a cap be fairer? Parties would still find ways around it.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Limits also ease the pressure to court large donors, which is another reason to have them.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: But limits restrict the ability of parties to talk to voters at all.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Capping spending forces parties to compete on ideas rather than on advertising budgets. In other words, a cap makes parties win arguments instead of buying airtime.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: I have volunteered for a party in two elections, so I have seen the work involved.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: What I mean is that a cap is just a cap on how many voters get informed.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Not so: limits can be set high enough that every party still runs a full campaign.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you can see that parties would still be able to reach every voter under limits of that kind. I read a report on it last winter.

utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Families need a fuller conversation about how children are doing.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: The district prints its report cards on pale blue paper. That detail is hardly central, but it is oddly familiar to parents.

utterances.text: Traditional report cards give families little explanation for the grades a child receives because schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences and because parents can ask follow-up questions during parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: A twice-yearly conference schedule gives every family two guaranteed conversations with teachers, which is another reason to make conferences the standard form of reporting.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: However, parent-teacher conferences take teachers away from lesson planning and marking, so replacing report cards would create a serious workload problem.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Because parents can ask follow-up questions, in other words, Annelise's proposal is that schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Parent-teacher conferences do not reveal the circumstances behind a child's academic performance. That limitation is a further reason to adopt the replacement.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My classroom does not have three windows, and the afternoon sun makes the projector difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: To put Annelise's proposal another way, it means making scheduled conversations the main form of reporting to parents.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Good evening, we are live from the old mill studio. Tonight's question: should households keep a shared emergency cash fund for unexpected expenses? Quentin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Every household should keep a shared emergency cash fund, because unexpected bills like a boiler failure arrive without warning.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: Jelena, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. Borrowing to cover a sudden bill costs far more than paying from savings, which is another reason. Mine lives in a biscuit tin, I admit.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: But a fund like that just sits idle. That is why inflation steadily erodes the value of cash.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, Clement, you think the money is wasted.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Every household should have one because a fund is insurance rather than an investment. Nobody judges a smoke alarm by its returns, after all.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: So you are saying, Valentina, that the fund should be judged by the protection it gives. We will take a vote after the break.
