utterances.text: Item two is the proposed ban on petrol leaf blowers and lawnmowers. Amara, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: I think we should prohibit them, because petrol garden machines release large quantities of carbon dioxide, which drives climate change.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: That is also a reason to ban them: petrol leaf blowers are far louder than residents find tolerable.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But a ban would hurt small landscaping firms that cannot afford electric equipment.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Not so, since the city could subsidise battery equipment for them.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So the city would pay for the switch, which makes sense because battery kit is cheaper to run than petrol kit.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: In other words, you want a phased ban over two years so firms can swap over gradually.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Noted. The council meets again on the first Thursday of next month.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Item two is the proposed ban on petrol leaf blowers and lawnmowers. Amara, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: I think we should prohibit them, because petrol garden machines emit large amounts of fine particulates and nitrogen oxides.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: That is also a reason to ban them: petrol leaf blowers are far louder than residents find tolerable.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But a ban would hurt small landscaping firms that cannot afford electric equipment.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Not so, since the city could subsidise battery equipment for them.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: My neighbour runs one of those firms, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So the city would pay for the switch, which makes sense because battery kit is cheaper to run than petrol kit.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: In other words, you want a phased ban over two years so firms can swap over gradually.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Noted. The council meets again on the first Thursday of next month.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: The parks department currently maintains the public lawns with a mix of petrol and battery mowers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should mobile operating systems be forced to allow alternative app stores? Ulla, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because the dominant app stores take up to thirty percent commission on every sale.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, you work with developers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I agree with Ulla, since developers have no realistic alternative way to reach customers. Also, competition between stores would push commissions down.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I do, because alternative stores would expose users to malware.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why are you so sure?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The platform owners' review process is what keeps phones safe, which is why that exposure matters. My niece lost her savings to a fake banking app last year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ulla?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Users could be forced onto risky stores to get the apps they want, since that is how it works for games. So, in other words, alternative stores would be dangerous for ordinary users.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Not entirely. Safety would remain in users' hands, as installing from outside the official store would need a deliberate warning-screen opt-in.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, a quick reply.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is no safeguard at all, because most people tap through warning screens without reading them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Europe has been through this.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Europe has already introduced rules of this kind.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Separately, sideloading is already common on desktop computers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Time is nearly up, so a last word. Ulla.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Do not adopt the rule, even with strong security standards.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Esther, would you let banks replace passwords with a scan of the customer's face?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes, banks should be allowed to, because passwords are routinely stolen or guessed.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But a leaked face cannot be reset the way a password can.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Banks keep only encrypted templates, not photographs, which is why a breach of that data would give thieves little.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying a breach of stored face data would not do much harm.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Exactly. Banks must require liveness checks, since spoofing with photos or masks is the real risk.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about customers who cannot use face login?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Customers must always be offered an alternative, because some have facial differences or disabilities that make scanning fail.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And what does it mean for the banks' costs?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: It would save them money on password resets, since they spend heavily on calls about forgotten passwords. That is another reason banks should be allowed to do it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, switching would cut their costs.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Yes. Banks should also require explicit consent before enrolling a face, since enrolling without it is a privacy violation.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The reason is that face enrolment should be opt-in only.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: That's right. I have used face unlock on my own phone for four years.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: So you are saying that the retention rule should come with a consistent national evidence standard.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: The community center is repainting its noticeboard this week.

utterances.text: Should businesses replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Yes. Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, because fixed allowances encourage employees to take days they do not need.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you think businesses should reconsider fixed holiday allowances because those allowances encourage unnecessary leave?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: That recommendation is too broad. On the contrary, the proposal is unlimited paid leave rather than compulsory leave-taking; in other words, employees would still choose when to be away.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: For context, I have eight years of experience working in human resources.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What would stop unlimited leave from making staffing unpredictable?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Shared team calendars make planned absences visible to managers, and because those absences are visible and because businesses should reconsider fixed holiday allowances because those allowances encourage unnecessary leave, managers can maintain adequate staffing under an unlimited-leave policy.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, unlimited paid leave is the proposed replacement for fixed holiday allowances.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Exactly. Unlimited paid leave is the proposed replacement for fixed holiday allowances, and it can reduce payments for unused holiday because employees are not building up a fixed bank of days.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Our office has a green reception desk.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I think election day should become a public holiday. The reason is that a public holiday would give shift workers time to vote.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Many hourly workers cannot leave work during polling hours. That is why a holiday would help people who are currently shut out.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: But employers would lose a day's output if election day became a public holiday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Existing early voting does not reach everyone, because thirty-eight percent of low-income voters skipped it in the last election.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: The election commission offers only two weeks of early voting. Many shift workers cannot attend early voting during those two weeks, which is another reason the current system has limited reach.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Hourly workers often cannot get away from work to vote. This supports the point that many hourly workers cannot leave work during polling hours.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: As a side note, my neighborhood holds a farmers' market every Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Marisol's concern about lost output is credible because small employers often cannot replace absent workers.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some countries that hold elections on holidays report higher turnout. A 2024 comparative study found higher average turnout in countries with election holidays, which is why I support considering the change.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: Put another way, international evidence links election holidays with higher turnout.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A public holiday would make voting a more visible civic event, and that visibility is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: A holiday would turn voting into a prominent shared civic occasion; that is what I mean by making voting more visible.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: However, a public holiday would not by itself guarantee high turnout. Turnout also depends on registration access and voter information, because people cannot vote if they are not prepared or registered.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: So the proposal is to give people a common day on which voting is easier and more visible.

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: For the record, my apartment building is repainting its entrance next month.

utterances.text: Our question is whether councils should let residents vote directly on how a fixed portion of the annual budget is spent. Chidi, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Residents should directly choose spending priorities for a fixed portion of the annual budget.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Participatory budgeting would allow residents to decide a defined portion of the annual budget, not the entire budget.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: To put my position plainly, direct resident voting should determine how a fixed share of the annual budget is spent. Because residents know their neighbourhood priorities, this would make council spending reflect local priorities more closely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: The reason to limit the scheme is that direct resident voting would give residents meaningful control without handing them the entire budget.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, participatory budgeting would let residents decide a defined slice of the annual budget rather than the whole budget. Because the slice is defined in advance, direct voting would be manageable for residents and councils.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: That boundary also protects funding for essential services, which is why limiting the vote to a defined budget slice matters.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Councils can publish costed options within legal limits before residents vote.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: So you are saying that residents could vote among options whose costs and legality had already been checked, because checked cost and legality information would help residents make realistic choices.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Pre-approved options would reduce the risk that residents vote for projects the council cannot deliver, because every option would have passed a basic feasibility check.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: My concern is that direct resident votes would mostly fund popular visible projects rather than essential maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: But that prediction is too strong: direct resident voting would not necessarily divert money from essential maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: The council's annual budget document is 180 pages long.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We have heard arguments about local control, safeguards, and the risk to less visible services.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: I have lived in the borough for six years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' relevant injury details before every game, because current pregame reports often use vague labels such as questionable without explaining a player's limitations.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because those labels are vague, fans cannot tell whether a player is likely to participate. That uncertainty therefore distorts public expectations about the game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Disclosing diagnoses when appropriate, expected minutes, and physical limitations would make injury reports useful. In other words, useful injury disclosure would explain what a player's participation actually means.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some injury details are private medical information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, a blanket disclosure rule could pressure players to compete while injured.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A narrower rule can protect diagnoses while requiring teams to report functional information. For that reason, the narrower rule justifies requiring teams to disclose relevant injury details before games.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author still keeps a paper ticket from a college basketball game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Transparent reports improve competitive fairness because opponents can prepare more accurately when they know which players are limited.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A useful report describes a player's capacity rather than merely listing participation status. That supports the claim that disclosing diagnoses when appropriate, expected minutes, and physical limitations would make injury reports useful.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author's favorite basketball arena serves unusually poor coffee.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A disclosure deadline several hours before tipoff would give opponents time to prepare, and that preparation would make the disclosure rule fairer.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put plainly, professional basketball teams should be required to disclose relevant player injury details before every game.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay that levy because unnecessary plastic packaging creates disposal costs for councils and households.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for imposing it?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A second reason is that a levy would encourage retailers to reduce unnecessary plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Some retailers say the levy would punish businesses that already operate on narrow profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: But that concern targets the wrong policy: the levy would target avoidable packaging rather than every package used by retailers, which is why retailers should pay that levy.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the levy cover protective wrapping as well as decorative wrapping?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: It should apply only to plastic packaging that is unnecessary for protecting or transporting fresh produce.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you mean that the levy would not apply to every piece of plastic packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers could avoid the levy by switching to reusable crates and lighter packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, retailers could escape the levy by using reusable crates and less packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Consumers should not bear the cost of unnecessary packaging through higher produce prices.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Elif is saying that shoppers should not pay for plastic packaging that retailers could avoid.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A levy based on packaging weight would be the simplest system to administer, because retailers can record packaging weight more easily than they can classify every design feature.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I buy fresh berries from a local shop every week. Retailers already record packaging weight for some supplier audits.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Because consumers should not bear the cost of unnecessary packaging through higher produce prices, the levy can be collected through existing packaging-data reports, which shows that most large retailers already submit those reports to regulators.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, existing packaging-data reports can be used to collect the levy, which is why retailers should pay it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would you support the proposal if the levy excluded genuinely necessary packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: I prefer buying loose apples when the shop has them.

utterances.text: I think cashless businesses should be required by law to accept physical money. The reason is that many elderly people and people without bank accounts cannot pay any other way.

utterances.text: But handling cash costs small businesses money in security and banking fees, which is why a mandate would be unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Our cafe went cashless two years ago, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: I don't think the burden is that unfair, since a small float and a locked tin cost very little.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Wanjiru, is that some customers have no alternative, so cash should be mandatory. That shows that handling cash costs small businesses money in security and banking fees.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Also card terminals go down in network outages, and cash is what keeps shops trading then, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The last outage in my town lasted most of a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Item four: satellite internet subsidies. Chloe, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Satellite internet providers currently serve customers in many countries around the world.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think governments should subsidise satellite internet for households without reliable broadband. Many rural households simply will not get any fixed-line connection in the next five years.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: But it would be wasted money, since fibre will reach most of those homes eventually.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: So you are saying, Josefa, that a satellite subsidy is short-term spending that fibre will make obsolete?

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Still, I accept that the rollout in remote areas has slipped by years more than once.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: My sister runs a farm shop and lost orders during an outage last winter.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Satellite dishes need a clear view of the sky to work.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Fine, then satellite could be a bridge for households until fibre arrives.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Put another way, it is a temporary measure that ends when fibre arrives.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: We could limit it to the dish and installation, since a one-off equipment subsidy would cost far less than paying monthly subscriptions.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Also, I should add that children in homes without broadband fall behind in schoolwork.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Satellite internet latency is higher than that of fixed-line connections.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Noted. Separately, the council should hold the next meeting in the town hall.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: Visiting cruise ships emit nitrogen oxides and fine particulates while they are berthed. Because those emissions affect residents near the waterfront, ports should impose binding emissions limits on visiting cruise ships.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Because of that policy, emissions limits on visiting cruise ships would reduce dockside pollution.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: For context, the port has fourteen cruise berths.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But cruise lines would divert ships to rival ports if emissions limits were imposed. That would put local jobs and visitor spending at risk.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A neighboring port kept its cruise traffic after imposing emissions limits and recorded lower dockside pollution. That example supports imposing limits, and it also confirms that limits reduce dockside pollution and supports the claim that the port has fourteen cruise berths.

utterances.speaker: Javier

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: The costs of installing shore-power equipment are manageable, which is another reason ports should impose emissions limits.

utterances.speaker: Samir
utterances.text: The port's annual cruise season runs from April through October.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: We have heard the environmental case, the concern about diverted ships, and evidence that cleaner port operations need not drive cruise traffic away.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, I believe terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because competent adults have authority over their own bodies and the manner of their deaths.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some patients have pain that palliative care simply cannot relieve, and that is why I say forcing them to endure it is cruel. Which is another reason the law should allow them to request help.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: But on the contrary, opponents say elderly and vulnerable people could feel pressured into choosing death, which is an objection to the point about unrelievable pain. But safeguards such as requiring two independent doctors make coercion much easier to detect.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has operated with such safeguards since 1997, which shows they work. Put another way, coercion is far easier to spot when two independent doctors must agree on a request.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Some people say good palliative care makes assisted dying unnecessary. But even the best hospices cannot relieve every patient's suffering, that is to say, medicine has limits.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I volunteered at a hospice for six years. The patients I met mostly wanted control over how their last days went, which shows how much people value authority over their own dying.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Legalising it would not oblige anyone to use it, since the right is only a right to request. In other words, nobody would be forced to take it up.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Hospice funding varies considerably from one region of Britain to another.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The bill debated last year ran to eleven pages, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Assisted dying has been debated in many parliaments around the world.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Public opinion supports it too, because recent polls show a large majority of British adults in favour.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: To sum up, patients deserve a lawful choice at the end of life.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This policy is necessary because some pupils arrive at school too hungry to concentrate well.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A second reason is that universal access to breakfast avoids marking some pupils as poor.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The primary schools in my district renovated their kitchens last year.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: School breakfast can help pupils begin the day ready to learn, which further supports this recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The case is stronger since providing breakfast at school can reduce the pressure on families during difficult mornings.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason to adopt the policy is that a universal breakfast programme is simpler to administer than a programme that checks family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually ate breakfast at home during primary school.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This recommendation is warranted because a free breakfast gives pupils a reliable opportunity to eat before lessons begin.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Finally, offering breakfast to all pupils can improve punctuality because children do not need to wait for food at home.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics raise one concern: universal breakfast provision would waste money on pupils from affluent families.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal breakfast provision would use public funds efficiently rather than waste money on pupils from affluent families.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, public schools should make free breakfast a universal service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In plain terms, every pupil should be able to eat breakfast at school without paying or proving low family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To state the proposal once more, schools should offer breakfast free to all pupils.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether emergency departments should charge patients who come in with non-urgent conditions. Amir, you start.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: I say yes, they should charge, because non-urgent patients make up about a third of attendances and they lengthen waits for everyone.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Ayesha, your response?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: A charge would deter poor patients from coming in even when their condition is serious.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So you are saying a charge would turn away people who truly need care.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: I would say no charge for non-urgent attendance, and that is why many people cannot get a same-day GP appointment. Wait, I mean the reason I say this is the first claim supports the second.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: I have worked as a triage nurse for twelve years. Let me tell you what I see.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Patients cannot reliably judge whether their condition is urgent, which is why a charge would be unfair to those who misjudge their symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Amir, do you have an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Charging would raise little money, but this is no surprise: collection systems in hospitals are expensive to run.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Put another way, a charge would send people away from care they need.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Next item: allowance versus paying for chores. Sipho, you start.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: I think parents should give a fixed weekly allowance and not pay for chores. It lets children practise budgeting, since they know in advance how much they will have.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Paying per chore has a worse effect, because children learn to expect payment for every household task.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: That is why they end up refusing to help at home when they do not need money, which is a reason to prefer the flat allowance.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Right, and doing chores is part of being a member of a family rather than a job, which is why paying for them is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Next door, the children quit doing the dishes as soon as they started being paid, which shows the problem is real.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: But paying for chores teaches that money is earned through effort, so I doubt a fixed allowance is better.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: A flat allowance teaches that money arrives regardless of effort, which is why that objection has some force.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: In other words, children paid per chore will skip tasks whenever they have enough money.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Noted. By the way, the heating in this room goes off at five.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: At home we used a flat allowance with a short list of unpaid jobs. My children now manage their money well and still help at home, which supports that mix.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: So you are saying a flat allowance plus unpaid chores gives both budgeting practice and a sense of family duty.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Yes. Let us also write a short leaflet for parents summarising this.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Many children spend most of their pocket money on snacks and games.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill, because a mandatory charge removes the diner's power to reward good service and penalise poor service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Without that power, servers have less incentive to try hard. And servers who try less hard give diners a worse experience.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I admit that many diners find tipping stressful and confusing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Automatic charges would spare diners the awkward arithmetic and social pressure of tipping.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But awkward arithmetic is a small price to pay for keeping control over what one pays.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once ate at a seaside cafe where the bill carried a charge of twelve percent.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Diners should be free to decide for themselves what a meal was worth.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: There is a second problem: restaurants that add automatic charges keep their menu prices artificially low.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Low menu prices mislead diners about what a meal will actually cost, which is why the practice is a bad one.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants that add automatic charges mislead diners about the true cost of a meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some restaurants pool the charge and share it among kitchen staff as well as servers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Pooling the charge is fairer to kitchen staff than leaving them with no share of tips.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a voluntary tip can still be pooled in the same way.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: My favourite waiter has worked at the same restaurant for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: So, to sum up, an optional, clearly suggested tip is the better compromise.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Pregnant patients sometimes cannot schedule antenatal appointments outside their working hours, and antenatal appointments can identify complications before they become emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That matters because unpaid time off for antenatal appointments can impose a financial penalty on pregnant patients.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Some employers would find universal paid time off difficult to administer. Even so, those practical concerns should not outweigh the case for employers offering pregnant patients paid time off for every antenatal appointment.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I keep my appointment reminders in a paper diary.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I would also include reasonable travel time, not just the consultation, in any paid entitlement.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That wider allowance is justified because antenatal appointments can involve unpredictable waiting times. It is also necessary since pregnant patients may have to travel a considerable distance to reach an antenatal clinic.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: So you are proposing paid time for the whole unavoidable journey and appointment, not merely the consultation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Yes, and paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Magnus means that every scheduled antenatal visit should qualify for paid time off. This supports the proposal that paid time off should be available for every scheduled antenatal appointment rather than only for scans or specialist visits. Put another way, Magnus is not limiting the entitlement to appointments that a manager considers medically important.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I think the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory entitlement could create an administrative burden for small employers, but that burden is not a reason to reject legal protection. A clear legal rule would give employers and pregnant patients consistent expectations because the entitlement to paid antenatal leave should be protected by law.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers should also allow pregnant patients some flexibility in choosing appointment times.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: That is practical because flexible scheduling can reduce disruption to colleagues and services.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The clinic near my home has green chairs in its waiting room.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Some antenatal clinics offer evening information sessions.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments cap the fees payment processors charge small businesses? Pradeep, you start.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Yes, they should. Small shops pay roughly three percent on every card sale, which takes up a big share of their thin profit margins.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Olumide, your reaction?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: And they cannot bargain, since small businesses have no power to negotiate fees with the processors.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a cap would make small merchants worse off, because it would push processors to drop the smallest merchants or cut services such as fraud protection.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I should say I used to own a bakery, so I have seen those statements first hand.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Processors will leave small businesses without services, which is why a cap is a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Petra, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Not really. Processors already compete for small merchants, and fees have fallen by a fifth in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small merchants are weak in bargaining and cannot compare offers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are running ten minutes over, so briefly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Petra, you are saying competition among processors is already keeping fees down.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, small merchants lack the bargaining power to negotiate fees.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: No, I mean a cap is justified only if processors are unconstrained, and they are not.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Fee caps in other countries have not caused processors to withdraw from small merchants.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should make landlords fit basic energy-saving measures before a rental licence is renewed. Priya, you start.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Councils should require it, because tenants in poorly insulated homes pay hundreds of pounds more a year on heating.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: But landlords will simply pass the cost on through higher rents. I should say I let out a flat myself.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, in other words, tenants would end up footing the bill anyway.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Basic measures would raise rents only modestly, since loft insulation and draught-proofing cost a landlord only a few hundred pounds; that is another reason to require them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Emeka, you have doubts of a different kind?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Enforcement is the real problem, because our council has two inspectors for 9,000 licensed homes.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: Put another way, Emeka, the rule would not exist on paper only.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Then licence fees should pay for more inspectors, since each renewal already brings in a fee.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying, Priya, that landlords' own fees should pay for the inspections.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Possibly, though my own council has just cut its housing budget.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should governments build desalination plants despite the energy use and marine impacts? Wilhelmina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because coastal cities cannot rely on rainfall alone as droughts grow longer and more frequent.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, what is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Desalination gives a supply that does not depend on rainfall, in other words a source that works through a drought.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: These plants burn enormous amounts of electricity, which is why they are too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tariq?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: But solar and wind farms built alongside them can power the plants, so the energy cost is largely removable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, a personal note?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: I have lived in a drought-hit town for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And the marine side?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Discharged brine makes the water saltier around outfalls and damages life on the seabed.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: That marine damage is a serious cost, since the brine harms the seabed.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Diffusers spreading brine over a wide area dilute it quickly, which is a reason to doubt how serious the damage is.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, alternatives?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Fixing leaking pipes would save more water than a new plant, because marine damage is a serious cost.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Let me sum up Gareth: so you are saying desalination is too energy-hungry to be a responsible choice, given huge electricity use.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: And Wilhelmina, so you are saying cities that are dry need a supply that does not depend on rainfall.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: The pipe-fixing programme in the region began last year.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: The first large desalination plants were built in the Middle East several decades ago.

utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether online voting should be introduced for national elections. Alina, you start.

utterances.text: Fatima, do you see other benefits?

utterances.text: Yes, since it would not make voting accessible to disabled people who struggle to reach polling stations, it is another reason to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: My neighbour once waited two hours at a polling station, I will say that much.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: I disagree, because online voting systems cannot be made secure enough for national elections, since hackers could alter votes without anyone noticing.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: But Estonia has operated online voting for many years with no proven tampering.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Astrid, the reason hackers could alter votes without anyone noticing is that online voting would let hostile actors alter results unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Since Estonia has operated online voting for many years with no proven tampering, online voting would let hostile actors alter results unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will return after the break.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Item two is the proposed ban on petrol leaf blowers and lawnmowers. Amara, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: I think we should prohibit them, because petrol garden machines emit large amounts of fine particulates and nitrogen oxides.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: That is also a reason to ban them: the noise from petrol leaf blowers is much louder than residents can reasonably put up with.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But a ban would hurt small landscaping firms that cannot afford electric equipment.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Not so, since the city could subsidise battery equipment for them.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: My neighbour runs one of those firms, as it happens, which shows that a ban would hurt small landscaping firms.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So the city would pay for the switch, which makes sense because battery kit is cheaper to run than petrol kit.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: In other words, you want a phased ban over two years so firms can swap over gradually.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Noted. The council meets again on the first Thursday of next month.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Separately, the council should publish the monthly air quality readings for the park.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight: should mobile operating systems be forced to allow alternative app stores? Ulla, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because the dominant app stores take up to thirty percent commission on every sale.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, you work with developers.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I agree with Ulla that mobile operating systems should be required to allow alternative app stores, which shows that developers have no realistic alternative way to reach customers. Also, competition between stores would lower the prices consumers pay for apps.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: I do, because alternative stores would expose users to malware.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Why are you so sure?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The platform owners' review process is what keeps phones safe, which is why that exposure matters. My niece lost her savings to a fake banking app last year.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ulla?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Users could be forced onto risky stores to get the apps they want, since that is how it works for games. So, in other words, alternative stores would be dangerous for ordinary users.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Not entirely. Safety would remain in users' hands, as installing from outside the official store would need a deliberate warning-screen opt-in.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, a quick reply.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: That is no safeguard at all, because most people tap through warning screens without reading them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Europe has been through this.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Europe has already introduced rules of this kind.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Time is nearly up, so a last word. Ulla.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Adopt the rule, with strong security standards.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Our question is whether pharmacies should prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. Thandiwe, why do you support the change?

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: Pharmacies should be allowed to prescribe routine antibiotics for minor infections without a doctor's appointment. The reason is that this would make treatment more accessible for people who cannot quickly see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I support the proposal because trained pharmacists can identify uncomplicated infections by using clear clinical protocols.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: But minor infection symptoms can conceal serious illnesses that require a doctor's examination. That risk makes prescribing at the pharmacy unsafe.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: A further reason for allowing the policy is that pharmacy prescribing would reduce pressure on already crowded general-practice appointments.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: Another reason is that a pharmacist can refer a patient to a doctor when the symptoms do not fit a routine infection.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Enzo, does the proposal include safeguards, or would every customer simply receive antibiotics?

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: The policy would apply only to uncomplicated cases assessed under an approved protocol.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: So you are saying the policy would be restricted to straightforward infections assessed under official clinical rules.

utterances.speaker: Enzo
utterances.text: Because the policy would be restricted to straightforward infections assessed under official clinical rules, every pharmacy taking part would need trained staff and a system for referring uncertain cases to doctors.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: In other words, participating pharmacies would require trained staff and a formal route for sending doubtful cases to doctors.

utterances.speaker: Thandiwe
utterances.text: The pharmacy near my home opens at seven o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: I have never liked the smell of antiseptic in medical waiting rooms.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Thank you. We have heard arguments about access, safeguards, and the danger of missing serious illness.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: I think schools should let students choose their own start times within a daily attendance window. This could improve attendance because students could align school with their sleep needs and family routines.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: I disagree. Schools need fixed start times to coordinate transportation reliably, because multiple bus departures would be difficult to coordinate if students arrived at different times.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: So you are saying that transportation problems make student-selected start times impractical?

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: In other words, my proposal is that students should be allowed to select their own start times within a defined attendance window.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: The school cafeteria currently serves breakfast from 7:45 onward.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: The arrangement remains workable because a staggered schedule could give teachers predictable groups of students. That works because predictable student groups would let teachers plan lessons more effectively.

utterances.speaker: Hamza
utterances.text: A shared attendance app could assign students to start-time groups automatically; because of that, teachers could plan around those groups, which is why schools can offer the choice. I have two younger siblings who attend primary school.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Schools should publish the daily attendance window on their websites.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays because those holidays require students to spend substantial time on worship and family observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I disagree: schools should keep homework deadlines during major religious holidays. The reason is that consistent deadlines prevent assignments from piling up afterward.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should require homework deadlines during major religious holidays. Many families plan their religious observances across several days, and that is another reason to adopt a ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students do not observe every major religious holiday. Several students also work part-time on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A homework ban would give students who observe religious holidays equal access to those holidays; this is another reason to adopt the ban. Equal access to religious observance matters because it is part of fair treatment at school.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A short holiday exemption could replace a complete homework ban. It would preserve time for essential coursework, which is why I prefer the exemption.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, your exemption proposal would still permit assignments during the holiday. Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays, and because of that, permitting assignments would still pressure students to choose schoolwork over religious observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Major religious holidays fall on different dates in different communities. Because of that, a single national homework ban would be difficult to schedule.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools can identify major religious holidays through published calendars, which makes a ban practical. In other words, published calendars allow schools to identify the holidays covered by the ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: To put your proposal another way, schools should suspend homework during major religious holidays. Put differently, one national ban would be hard to schedule across communities with different holiday dates.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools in some districts have four-day instructional weeks.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students commute to school by bus.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: School classrooms often have windows.

utterances.text: I disagree: schools should keep homework deadlines during major religious holidays. The reason is that consistent deadlines prevent assignments from piling up afterward.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that schools should require homework deadlines during major religious holidays. Many families plan their religious observances across several days, and that is another reason to adopt a ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Some students do not observe every major religious holiday. Several students also work part-time on weekends.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A homework ban would give students who observe religious holidays equal access to those holidays; this is another reason to adopt the ban. Equal access to religious observance matters because it is part of fair treatment at school.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A short holiday exemption could replace a complete homework ban. It would preserve time for essential coursework, which is why I prefer the exemption.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, your exemption proposal would still permit assignments during the holiday. Permitting assignments would still pressure students to choose schoolwork over religious observance, and that is why I support a full ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Major religious holidays fall on different dates in different communities. Because of that, a single national homework ban would be difficult to schedule.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Because some students do not observe every major religious holiday, schools can identify major religious holidays through published calendars, which makes a ban practical. In other words, published calendars allow schools to identify the holidays covered by the ban.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: To put your proposal another way, schools should suspend homework during major religious holidays. Put differently, one national ban would be hard to schedule across communities with different holiday dates.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The central reason is that plurality voting can elect a legislator without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That happens because splitting votes among several candidates can allow a candidate opposed by most voters to win under plurality voting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Under ranked-choice voting, a voter's ballot transfers to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: This gives voters a way to support a preferred candidate without wasting their vote if that candidate is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting can produce a winner with support from voters whose first choices were eliminated; this supports the preceding claim.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a winner with support from transferred ballots has a broader mandate than a winner elected only through a plurality of first-choice votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics are right that replacing plurality voting could make elections confusing for voters, but that objection does not outweigh the democratic benefit; this concern is an objection to the claim that a winner with support from transferred ballots has a broader mandate than a winner elected only through a plurality of first-choice votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The reason for the concern is that voters may need to understand several preferences and the elimination process in a ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That process gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters; in other words, ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice voting gives the eventual winner support beyond the winner's initial first-choice voters, ranked-choice voting transfers a voter's ballot to a later preference when the voter's preferred candidate is eliminated; this is the same transfer rule described earlier.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Legislative elections determine who writes and votes on laws.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Some voters prefer to read policy platforms before choosing a candidate.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing election software can record and process ranked ballots, which is why ranked-choice voting transfers ballots according to voters' later preferences after weaker candidates are eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many legislative districts have fixed geographic boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I think farmers should be banned from spraying organophosphates within 200 metres of schools and playgrounds. The reason is that children's developing bodies are more sensitive to these chemicals than adults' are.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Spray drift from the fields also regularly reaches playgrounds, which is a second reason.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But a 200-metre buffer would take a big share of the land from farmers with small plots right beside villages.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I grew up on a farm, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Wind-direction rules are enough, which shows that spraying only when the wind blows away from buildings keeps drift off playgrounds, and that is a reason why farmers should be banned from spraying organophosphates within 200 metres of schools and playgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: So what you mean, Xavier, is that wind-direction rules alone would be enough.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Residues have turned up in playground dust 150 metres from sprayed fields, which shows drift really does reach children. Also, my cousin teaches at a primary school in the next county.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I could accept a buffer if the state compensated farmers, since the loss of land would fall on them alone.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: In other words, you would back the buffer provided the state pays farmers for the lost land.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I can live with that. The state already pays crop subsidies and could cover the compensation, and the reason is that Xavier would accept a buffer if the state compensated farmers.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. I support the proposal, and five years of service is a reasonable threshold for sabbatical eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Employees should be allowed to take paid sabbaticals after five years of service, because five years is a reasonable threshold for eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: I agree with the principle. Paid sabbaticals can help employees return with renewed energy and useful skills, so the policy would benefit both staff and organisations.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: But small employers may struggle to cover an employee's duties during a paid sabbatical. That practical burden makes a universal entitlement risky.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A consistent sabbatical policy can help organisations keep experienced employees. Since replacing skilled staff is expensive, retention is an important benefit.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: To put it another way, Hector's proposal would give employees a paid break after five years of service.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: The proposal that employees should be allowed to take paid sabbaticals after five years of service supports my view that five years is a reasonable threshold for granting paid sabbaticals. I still think employers should be allowed to set blackout periods during peak seasons.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: For context, I have worked in human-resources policy for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: One small observation: the studio lights have become noticeably warmer during this debate.

utterances.text: And they cannot bargain, since small businesses have no power to negotiate fees with the processors.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: But a cap would make small merchants worse off, because it would push processors to drop the smallest merchants or cut services such as fraud protection.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I should say I used to own a bakery, so I have seen those statements first hand.

utterances.speaker: Olumide

utterances.speaker: Host

utterances.text: Not really. Processors already compete for small merchants, and fees have fallen by a fifth in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small merchants are weak in bargaining and cannot compare offers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are running ten minutes over, so briefly.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Petra, you are saying competition among processors is already keeping fees down.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, small merchants do not have the bargaining strength to negotiate fees.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Small merchants lack that power since a cap on fees is justified because processors are not constrained by anyone.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Fee caps in other countries have not caused processors to withdraw from small merchants.

utterances.text: Tonight: should cricket teams be allowed substitutes specifically for concussion? Milos, you start.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because a concussed batter who stays on the field risks serious long-term brain injury.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Hollis, where do you stand on this?

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Players hide their symptoms because they do not want to let their team down. A replacement means teams would be less likely to pressure a concussed player to carry on, and that is why I back it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: But replacements would be open to abuse by teams faking head knocks to bring on a specialist bowler. I played club cricket for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Milos, can that be answered?

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Yes, because match referees could check each case, so a faked head knock would not succeed.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying a referee's check would stop fake claims?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Concussion symptoms can appear hours after the blow, so a quick check on the field can miss them. In other words, referee checks are unreliable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will take a break. The next international series starts in March.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Fine, but the whole question is about fairness rather than safety.

utterances.text: Item two is the proposed ban on petrol leaf blowers and lawnmowers. Amara, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: But a ban would hurt small landscaping firms that cannot afford electric equipment.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Not so, since the city could subsidise battery equipment for them.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: My neighbour runs one of those firms, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So the city would pay for the switch, which makes sense because battery kit is cheaper to run than petrol kit.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: In other words, you want the city to ban petrol machines only for commercial landscapers, while leaving households free to use them.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Separately, several neighbouring councils have already introduced restrictions on petrol garden equipment.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Noted. The council meets again on the first Thursday of next month.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: I think hospitals should use AI to prioritise patients for scarce treatments, because an AI system applies the same criteria to every patient, whereas tired clinicians vary from one shift to the next.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: So you are saying that AI ranking would be more consistent than ranking by clinicians.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: But an AI system would reproduce past inequalities in its rankings, since these tools are trained on historical records that reflect past under-treatment of some groups.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Quick aside: I work night shifts on a cardiology ward, so I have seen how the variation plays out.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A hospital in the Netherlands audited its triage model every quarter and corrected the bias it found, because regular audits can catch and correct bias in an AI triage model. That general point is a reason to support using AI for prioritisation.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Fair point. I would add that AI prioritisation is only acceptable if its rankings can be audited.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: I should say I have not actually seen the tool you both keep mentioning.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: In other words, the rankings would be open to audit, and that makes AI prioritisation acceptable.
